problem_statement:
Title: Reverse time zone conversion for "Etc/GMT-*" zones in Trunc()/Extract (Postgres) after Django 3.2

Description
When passing a tzinfo like pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10") (or zoneinfo.ZoneInfo("Etc/GMT-10")) to Trunc()/Extract via the TimezoneMixin, the SQL generated for Postgres AT TIME ZONE is incorrect in Django 3.2 compared to Django 3.1.

Summary of the behavior observed:
- In Django 3.1, timezone._get_timezone_name(pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10")) returned "+10". Postgres DatabaseOperations._prepare_tzname_delta() then turned that into "-10" in the AT TIME ZONE clause, producing:
  SELECT ... DATE_TRUNC('day', "my_model"."start_at" AT TIME ZONE '-10') AS "date" ...
  This corresponds to 10 hours east of UTC (Etc/GMT-10).
- In Django 3.2, timezone._get_timezone_name(pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10")) returns "Etc/GMT-10" instead of "+10". DatabaseOperations._prepare_tzname_delta() then produces "Etc/GMT+10" in the SQL, producing:
  SELECT ... DATE_TRUNC('day', "my_model"."start_at" AT TIME ZONE 'Etc/GMT+10') AS "date" ...
  This is effectively the opposite sign and therefore the wrong direction (10 hours west instead of east).

Concrete REPL examples that motivated this report:
- Django 3.1
  >>> timezone._get_timezone_name(pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10"))
  '+10'
- Django 3.2
  >>> timezone._get_timezone_name(pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10"))
  'Etc/GMT-10'

This difference is the same when using Python's zoneinfo.ZoneInfo('Etc/GMT-10').

Why this matters
- For `Etc/GMT-<n>` zone names, the sign semantics are reversed in the zone name (Etc/GMT-10 actually means UTC−10), so generating the numeric offset or the correct AT TIME ZONE operand is delicate. The change in _get_timezone_name() return value appears to interact with Postgres-specific timestamp SQL generation and ends up flipping the direction of the timezone when rendered in SQL.

Expected behavior
- For a tzinfo representing "Etc/GMT-10" (10 hours east of UTC in the "Etc" naming scheme), the generated SQL should use the offset that yields the intended conversion direction. For the above example the SQL AT TIME ZONE operand should correspond to -10 (or a representation that Postgres understands as 10 hours east), not "Etc/GMT+10" which reverses the direction.

Observed behavior
- After the change, the SQL sometimes contains the reversed sign variant (e.g. "Etc/GMT+10") and produces the opposite time conversion.

Tentative Reproducing Test
The following pytest-style test is a starting point to demonstrate the mismatch between the timezone name produced by Django's timezone utilities and the Postgres operations code that prepares the AT TIME ZONE operand.

This is a starting point test (not a full test-suite-ready or DB-dependent test). It inspects the values produced by timezone._get_timezone_name and DatabaseOperations._prepare_tzname_delta and asserts the SQL operand is the expected numeric offset form for "Etc/GMT-10".

Note: This test assumes the Django version under test exposes timezone._get_timezone_name and the Postgres DatabaseOperations._prepare_tzname_delta method. It is intended to illustrate the problem and produce an assertion showing actual vs expected output.

import pytest
import pytz
from django.utils import timezone

# Import the Postgres DatabaseOperations class; depending on Django internals this import path is stable:
from django.db.backends.postgresql.operations import DatabaseOperations

try:
    # Python 3.9+ zoneinfo
    from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
except Exception:
    ZoneInfo = None

def test_prepare_tzname_delta_for_etc_gmt_minus_10():
    """
    Starting-point test to demonstrate the reported mismatch.

    Expected: For tz "Etc/GMT-10" we expect the SQL AT TIME ZONE operand to be the numeric
    offset that corresponds to 10 hours east (commonly rendered as '-10' in the AT TIME ZONE clause).
    Observed: In some Django versions/configurations this becomes 'Etc/GMT+10' (the opposite sign).
    """
    tz_pytz = pytz.timezone("Etc/GMT-10")
    tzname_from_django = timezone._get_timezone_name(tz_pytz)
    ops = DatabaseOperations()
    sql_operand = ops._prepare_tzname_delta(tzname_from_django)

    # The expected AT TIME ZONE operand for "Etc/GMT-10" (10 hours east) — adjust if your environment expects a different canonical representation.
    expected_sql_operand = "-10"

    # If zoneinfo is available, show the same flow for ZoneInfo
    if ZoneInfo is not None:
        tz_zoneinfo = ZoneInfo("Etc/GMT-10")
        tzname_zoneinfo = timezone._get_timezone_name(tz_zoneinfo)
        sql_operand_zoneinfo = ops._prepare_tzname_delta(tzname_zoneinfo)
    else:
        tzname_zoneinfo = None
        sql_operand_zoneinfo = None

    # Build a sample SQL snippet to illustrate the final rendering:
    sample_sql = "DATE_TRUNC('day', \"my_model\".\"start_at\" AT TIME ZONE '{}') AS \"date\"".format(sql_operand)

    # Assert (this is the part that will fail in environments exhibiting the bug).
    # The failing assertion will show actual vs expected.
    assert sql_operand == expected_sql_operand, (
        "Unexpected AT TIME ZONE operand produced.\n"
        "tzinfo: {!r}\n"
        "timezone._get_timezone_name(...) returned: {!r}\n"
        "DatabaseOperations._prepare_tzname_delta(...) returned: {!r}\n"
        "Expected AT TIME ZONE operand: {!r}\n"
        "Example SQL fragment that would be generated:\n    {}\n"
        "ZoneInfo path (if available) produced tzname={!r}, operand={!r}"
        .format(tz_pytz, tzname_from_django, sql_operand, expected_sql_operand, sample_sql, tzname_zoneinfo, sql_operand_zoneinfo)
    )

# End of starting-point test

problem_statement:
Issue summary

When rendering a ForeignKey field as a readonly field in a custom AdminSite, the admin helper that builds the link to the related object generates a URL in the "admin" namespace (e.g. /admin/...) instead of using the custom AdminSite namespace (e.g. /custom-admin/...). In other words, the link points to the default admin site rather than the currently active custom admin site.

Root cause (investigation)

In django.contrib.admin.helpers.get_admin_url the URL is created with a call like:
    url = reverse(url_name, args=[quote(remote_obj.pk)])
but that call does not include the current_app keyword argument. Other parts of the admin code pass current_app=self.model_admin.admin_site.name when reversing named admin URLs (for example, ModelAdmin.response_add). Because current_app is not passed, the reverse call resolves the URL against the default admin namespace ('admin') instead of the name of the custom AdminSite currently being used.

Proposed local fix

I was able to make this specific case behave correctly by changing the reverse call to include current_app from the ModelAdmin's AdminSite:
    url = reverse(
        url_name,
        args=[quote(remote_obj.pk)],
        current_app=self.model_admin.admin_site.name
    )

I haven't run the full Django test suite to verify there are no regressions or side effects, so I'm sharing this to ask for feedback: is passing current_app here the right approach? Are there any reasons get_admin_url shouldn't use the model_admin.admin_site.name when reversing URLs?

Tentative Reproducing Test

Below is a pytest-style test that demonstrates the problem by checking whether get_admin_url passes the current_app argument into django.urls.reverse. This is a starting point for reproducing the bug in a Django project and is not a complete fix or final test suite.

The test monkeypatches django.urls.reverse to capture the keyword arguments used when get_admin_url calls reverse:
- Expected behavior: current_app should equal the custom AdminSite.name (e.g. "custom_admin").
- Actual (buggy) behavior: current_app will be None / not provided, indicating get_admin_url did not pass the AdminSite name to reverse.

Note: This test assumes you are running it inside a Django test environment (pytest-django) and that django.contrib.admin.helpers.get_admin_url exists. It is intended as a starting point to reproduce and assert the bug, not as a full production test.

Tentative Reproducing Test (starting point)

def test_get_admin_url_passes_current_app(monkeypatch, db):
    """
    Starting point test: ensure get_admin_url passes current_app to django.urls.reverse.

    Expected:
        - get_admin_url should call reverse(..., current_app=custom_admin.name)

    Actual (observed in the buggy behavior):
        - reverse is called without current_app (or current_app is None),
          which causes URLs to be generated in the default 'admin' namespace.
    """
    from django.contrib.admin.sites import AdminSite
    from django.contrib.admin.options import ModelAdmin
    from django.contrib.admin.helpers import get_admin_url
    from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model

    called = {}

    # Monkeypatch django.urls.reverse to capture keyword args passed to it.
    def fake_reverse(name, *args, **kwargs):
        called['name'] = name
        called['kwargs'] = kwargs
        # Return a sentinel URL so get_admin_url returns something runnable.
        return '/fake-url/'

    monkeypatch.setattr('django.urls.reverse', fake_reverse)

    # Create a custom admin site with a non-default name.
    custom_site = AdminSite(name='custom_admin')

    # Use a real model class (User) and attach a ModelAdmin to the custom site.
    User = get_user_model()
    model_admin = ModelAdmin(User, custom_site)

    # Create an instance (requires DB).
    user = User.objects.create_user(username='tester', password='password')

    # Call the helper under test.
    url = get_admin_url(user, model_admin)

    # Basic sanity: get_admin_url should still return the fake URL we provided.
    assert url == '/fake-url/', f"Unexpected return from fake_reverse: {url!r}"

    # EXPECTED: current_app should be set to the custom admin site name.
    expected_current_app = custom_site.name

    # Show actual vs expected for debugging: if this assertion fails, the test demonstrates the bug.
    actual_current_app = called.get('kwargs', {}).get('current_app', None)
    assert actual_current_app == expected_current_app, (
        "get_admin_url did not pass current_app to django.urls.reverse. "
        f"Expected current_app={expected_current_app!r}, got {actual_current_app!r}. "
        "This causes links to be resolved in the default admin namespace instead of the custom AdminSite."
    )

problem_statement:
Title: ModelChoiceIteratorValue is unhashable after upgrading to Django 3.1

Description
I upgraded a project from Django 3.0 to Django 3.1. I override the Select.create_option method to add custom data-* attributes to option tags. After the upgrade some select options started raising:

TypeError: unhashable type: 'ModelChoiceIteratorValue'

The problematic code looks like this:

def create_option(self, name, value, label, selected, index, subindex=None, attrs=None):
    context = super().create_option(name, value, label, selected, index, subindex, attrs)
    if not value:
        return context
    if value in self.show_fields:  # self.show_fields is a dict keyed by integer PKs, e.g. {1: ['first_name', 'last_name']}
        context['attrs']['data-fields'] = json.dumps(self.show_fields[value])

Prior to Django 3.1 this membership check worked as expected. In Django 3.1 the value passed into create_option for ModelChoiceField options is a ModelChoiceIteratorValue instance that (in this version) is not hashable. The "if value in self.show_fields" line triggers a TypeError because dict.__contains__ needs to hash the lookup object. Note that doing the same check against a list of integers (value in allowed_values where allowed_values is a list like [1, 2]) does not raise — because list membership uses equality checks and does not require hashing of the looked-up object.

Expected behavior
- Either ModelChoiceIteratorValue should be hashable and compare equal to the underlying PK (so "if value in {1:...}" works), or the value passed to create_option should be a hashable type (e.g. the raw PK) so existing custom create_option implementations don't break.

Actual behavior
- In Django 3.1, ModelChoiceIteratorValue is unhashable, causing "if value in dict" checks to raise TypeError.

Workarounds
- Convert the value to its underlying pk before checking membership (e.g. int(value) or str(value) depending on your keys) inside create_option.
- This rewrite and the test below are provided to reproduce the issue and demonstrate the failure.

Tentative Reproducing Test
This is a starting-point pytest test that demonstrates the issue. It constructs a ModelChoiceIteratorValue (the same type Django provides to option creation logic) and performs a membership check against a dict keyed by integer PKs. The test documents the expected behavior (no TypeError and membership resolves True) and fails with a clear message if a TypeError is raised (the observed bug).

Note: This is a minimal reproducer — adapt into your test suite or wrap in Django test setup if you want to exercise the full widget create_option path.

import pytest
from django.forms.models import ModelChoiceIteratorValue

def test_modelchoiceiteratorvalue_membership_against_int_key_starting_point():
    """
    Starting point reproducer for:
    TypeError: unhashable type: 'ModelChoiceIteratorValue'
    
    Expected (pre-3.1 behavior): checking 'value in {1: ...}' should not raise and should evaluate to True
    Actual (observed on affected versions): a TypeError is raised because ModelChoiceIteratorValue is not hashable.
    """
    # Create a ModelChoiceIteratorValue that wraps PK=1 (second arg can be any object)
    value = ModelChoiceIteratorValue(1, object())
    show_fields = {1: ['first_name', 'last_name']}

    # Expected: no TypeError, membership check returns True
    try:
        contains = value in show_fields
    except TypeError as exc:
        pytest.fail(
            "Actual: TypeError raised when checking membership: {!s}. "
            "Expected: no TypeError; ModelChoiceIteratorValue should be usable in 'value in {{1:...}}' checks "
            "(either by being hashable or by comparing to the underlying PK). "
            "This reproduces the bug observed after upgrading to Django 3.1.".format(exc)
        )

    assert contains is True, (
        "Expected ModelChoiceIteratorValue(1, ...) to be considered equal to key 1 in the dict. "
        "If this assertion fails, the behavior differs from the pre-3.1 expectation."
    )

This test is a starting point, not a final solution. It highlights the discrepancy between expected and actual behavior and should help reproduce the issue in a CI environment running the affected Django version.

A RenameModel operation that targets a model which already sets an explicit db_table should not change the database schema.

Rationale:
- When a Django model defines Meta.db_table, the database table name is fixed and independent of the model class name. Renaming the Python model class (via a RenameModel migration operation) should be a no-op at the database level because the underlying table name does not change.
- Currently, executing RenameModel against a model with db_table set is not a no-op:
  - On PostgreSQL backends, Django drops and recreates foreign key constraints.
  - On SQLite backends, Django recreates the table (which is disruptive and unnecessary).

Expected behavior:
- If the model before and after the rename have the same db_table option, the RenameModel operation should not emit any schema-changing SQL or otherwise alter database objects.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — not a final solution, intended to reproduce the issue.
# This pytest-style test assumes a Django test environment. It collects SQL emitted
# by the migration operation and asserts that no SQL should be produced when the
# model defines an explicit db_table that does not change.

import pytest

pytest.importorskip("django")  # skip if Django is not available

from django.db import connection, models
from django.db.migrations.state import ProjectState, ModelState
from django.db.migrations.operations import RenameModel

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_rename_model_with_db_table_is_noop():
    """
    Create two project states that differ only by the model class name but have
    the same Meta.db_table. Run RenameModel.database_forwards with a schema
    editor that collects SQL and assert that no SQL is emitted.

    Expected: editor.collected_sql == []
    Actual (bug): editor.collected_sql contains CREATE/ALTER statements (table recreated or FKs dropped/created)
    """

    app_label = "myapp"
    old_name = "OldName"
    new_name = "NewName"
    custom_table = "custom_table"

    # Define a simple model state with an explicit db_table
    fields = [("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True))]
    from_model = ModelState(app_label, old_name, fields=fields, options={"db_table": custom_table})
    to_model = ModelState(app_label, new_name, fields=fields, options={"db_table": custom_table})

    # Build project states containing the single model
    from_state = ProjectState()
    from_state.add_model_state(from_model)
    to_state = ProjectState()
    to_state.add_model_state(to_model)

    op = RenameModel(old_name, new_name)

    # Collect SQL produced by the operation without executing it
    with connection.schema_editor(collect_sql=True) as editor:
        op.database_forwards(app_label, editor, from_state, to_state)
        collected = list(editor.collected_sql)

    # This is the assertion that demonstrates the bug when it fails:
    # If RenameModel is correctly a no-op for models with db_table set, there should be no SQL.
    assert collected == [], (
        "Expected no SQL to be emitted for RenameModel on a model with an explicit db_table, "
        f"but collected SQL statements were found: {collected}"
    )

problem_statement:
Summary
When using Django admin search_fields that include related-field lookups (e.g. 'clientoffice__name'), a multi-word search causes the changelist queryset to generate a JOIN for each search token. For long queries (more than ~3 words) this produces many redundant JOINs and can stall the admin page.

Environment
- Django 1.2.5 (original report)
- Models involved: Client and ClientOffice (ClientOffice has a ForeignKey to Client)
- Admin: ClientAdmin.search_fields includes both Client fields and related lookups:
  ('name', 'name2', 'contact_person', 'clientoffice__name', 'clientoffice__name2')

Observed numbers from the reporter (for context)
- Client.objects.count() == 10907
- ClientOffice.objects.count() == 16952

Steps to reproduce (high level)
1. Register ClientAdmin with search_fields that include clientoffice__name and clientoffice__name2.
2. Go to the admin changelist for Client and enter a search query containing several words (more than 3).
3. The admin page stalls / performs very slowly.

Root cause hypothesis
The admin search implementation loops over search terms and repeatedly narrows the queryset using qs = qs.filter(...). For related lookups this pattern accumulates JOINs: each iteration adds another JOIN to the same related table instead of reusing the existing JOIN. The final SQL ends up with many duplicate JOIN clauses, one per search token, which is inefficient and can lead to very slow queries.

Patch note
The reporter attached a patch for Django 1.2.5 to avoid building duplicate JOINs; adapting that approach to later versions should be straightforward (the fix is to build combined OR/AND clauses without repeatedly rejoining the same table).

Tentative Reproducing Test
The following pytest-style test is a starting point that demonstrates the issue by inspecting the generated SQL for repeated JOIN keywords (or repeated occurrences of the related table name). You will need to adapt the imports and app/model names to your project. This is a starting point for reproducing and asserting the problematic behavior; it may require adjustment for different Django versions.

Note: replace 'myapp' with the actual app label where Client and ClientOffice are defined.

from django.test import RequestFactory
import pytest
from django.contrib import admin

# Replace these imports with the real locations of your models.
from myapp.models import Client, ClientOffice
from myapp.admin import ClientAdmin  # or recreate the admin class inline if needed

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_admin_search_generates_duplicate_joins():
    """
    Starting-point test to demonstrate that a multi-word admin search
    that includes related lookups can produce repeated JOINs in the SQL.

    Expected behavior (what we want):
    - The SQL should contain at most one JOIN to the clientoffice table
      regardless of how many search tokens are provided.

    Actual behavior (what this test checks for):
    - The SQL contains more than one JOIN (one per search token), indicating
      redundant JOINs are being added.

    This test constructs a small dataset, instantiates the ModelAdmin, calls
    get_search_results, inspects str(qs.query) and counts occurrences of
    'JOIN' (or the related table name). Adjust the assertions depending on
    your Django version and exact SQL dialect.
    """
    # Create minimal data
    client = Client.objects.create(name="Alpha", name2="", contact_person="Alice")
    ClientOffice.objects.create(client=client, name="Office1", name2="")
    ClientOffice.objects.create(client=client, name="Office2", name2="")

    # Instantiate admin and prepare a fake request
    rf = RequestFactory()
    request = rf.get('/admin/myapp/client/')
    # If your ClientAdmin class isn't available, you can build one inline:
    # class SimpleClientAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    #     search_fields = ('name', 'name2', 'contact_person', 'clientoffice__name', 'clientoffice__name2')
    # admin_instance = SimpleClientAdmin(Client, admin.site)
    admin_instance = ClientAdmin(Client, admin.site)

    # Use a multi-word search; original report mentioned >3 words triggers the issue
    search_query = "one two three four"

    # get_search_results returns (qs, use_distinct)
    qs, use_distinct = admin_instance.get_search_results(request, Client.objects.all(), search_query)

    sql = str(qs.query).lower()

    # Count JOIN occurrences (simple heuristic). You can also count occurrences of the related table name.
    join_count = sql.count(' join ')
    related_table_occurrences = sql.count('clientoffice')  # adjust table name if migration adds app label prefix

    # Debug output (useful when running the test)
    print("Generated SQL:", sql)
    print("JOIN count:", join_count)
    print("Related table occurrences:", related_table_occurrences)

    # This assertion demonstrates the problematic condition: more than one JOIN.
    # In a correct implementation we'd expect <= 1 JOIN to the related table.
    assert join_count > 1, (
        "Test is a starting point: expected to see multiple JOINs for a multi-word "
        "search that includes related lookups; if this fails on your version of Django, "
        "the query planner or ORM may already avoid duplicate JOINs."
    )

    # Optionally assert that the related table appears multiple times (another heuristic)
    # Note: Depending on your DB table naming (app_model), adjust the string checked above.
    assert related_table_occurrences > 1 or join_count > 1, (
        "Expected repeated occurrences of the related table or multiple JOINs in the SQL."
    )

# End of tentative reproducing test

problem_statement:
When inspectdb encounters a foreign key that references a non-primary but UNIQUE column on another table, it doesn't record the referenced field in the generated model code.

Example database schema that triggers the problem (PostgreSQL):

CREATE TABLE foo (
    id serial primary key,
    other_id int UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE bar (
    id serial primary key,
    other_id int,
    constraint myconst
        FOREIGN KEY(other_id) references foo(other_id)
);

Expected behavior:
- The generated model for bar.other_id should be a ForeignKey to Foo that explicitly points to the non-primary referenced field (other_id), e.g. include to_field='other_id' (and db_column='other_id' as appropriate).

Actual behavior:
- inspectdb generates a ForeignKey to Foo without the to_field argument, which implies a reference to Foo's primary key rather than the UNIQUE other_id column, producing incorrect models for this schema.

I am attaching a tentative fix separately; I didn't have time to add unit tests then.

Tentative Reproducing Test

Below is a pytest-style test (starting point) that demonstrates the issue by:
- creating the two tables directly via raw SQL,
- running Django's inspectdb management command and capturing its output,
- asserting that the generated model contains a to_field='other_id' on the ForeignKey (the expected behavior).

This test is a starting point and may need environment adjustments (database backend/settings). It is written for PostgreSQL and requires pytest-django (or another way to provide a configured Django test DB). It intentionally asserts the expected behavior; on the current failing implementation this test should fail, showing the difference between expected and actual output.

Starting point test (pytest):

import io
import pytest
from django.core.management import call_command
from django.db import connection, transaction

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_inspectdb_preserves_foreign_key_to_unique_field():
    """
    Starting point test: create two tables where bar.other_id is a FK to foo.other_id (a UNIQUE non-PK),
    run inspectdb, and assert that the generated model for bar contains to_field='other_id'.

    Notes:
    - This test assumes a Django test database is available and that the DB backend supports the SQL used.
    - It is written with PostgreSQL in mind. Adjust SQL if using a different backend.
    - This is a minimal reproduction: it creates/drops tables in the test database.
    """
    create_foo = "CREATE TABLE foo (id serial primary key, other_id int UNIQUE);"
    create_bar = (
        "CREATE TABLE bar ("
        "id serial primary key, "
        "other_id int, "
        "CONSTRAINT myconst FOREIGN KEY (other_id) REFERENCES foo(other_id)"
        ");"
    )
    drop_bar = "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS bar;"
    drop_foo = "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS foo;"

    cursor = connection.cursor()
    try:
        # Ensure clean state
        cursor.execute(drop_bar)
        cursor.execute(drop_foo)
        # Create tables
        cursor.execute(create_foo)
        cursor.execute(create_bar)
        # Commit DDL if needed
        transaction.get_connection().commit()

        # Run inspectdb and capture output
        out = io.StringIO()
        call_command('inspectdb', stdout=out)
        output = out.getvalue()

        # The expected snippet: the ForeignKey for other_id should include to_field='other_id'
        expected = "to_field='other_id'"

        # For debugging, include the generated section for the bar model if assertion fails.
        if expected not in output:
            # Optionally narrow down the generated model for bar to help debug
            start_marker = "class Bar"
            bar_section = output.split(start_marker, 1)[-1] if start_marker in output else output
            raise AssertionError(
                f"inspectdb did not include {expected} in generated models.\n"
                f"Full output:\n{output}\n\n"
                f"Bar model section (approx):\n{bar_section}"
            )

    finally:
        # Clean up
        try:
            cursor.execute(drop_bar)
            cursor.execute(drop_foo)
            transaction.get_connection().commit()
        except Exception:
            # Best-effort cleanup; ignore errors to not mask the original assertion
            pass

problem_statement:
Summary
i18n_patterns does not recognize language locale tags that include both a script and a region subtag (e.g. en-latn-us or en-Latn-US). Routes generated by i18n_patterns are available for simple language tags like en-us, but requests to en-latn-us or en-Latn-US return 404.

What I did
- settings.py
  - LANGUAGE_CODE = 'en-us'
  - LANGUAGES = [
      ('en-us', "English"),
      ('en-latn-us', "Latin English"),
      ('en-Latn-US', "BCP 47 case format"),
    ]
  - added 'django.middleware.locale.LocaleMiddleware' to MIDDLEWARE

- urls.py
  - used i18n_patterns to wrap a simple view:
    from django.conf.urls.i18n import i18n_patterns
    from django.http import HttpResponse
    from django.urls import path

    def bangiah(request):
        return HttpResponse('U!')

    urlpatterns += i18n_patterns(
        path('', bangiah),
    )

Observed behavior
- GET /en-us/ → 200, "U!"
- GET /en-latn-us/ → 404 Not Found
- GET /en-Latn-US/ → 404 Not Found

Expected behavior
- GET /en-latn-us/ → 200, "U!"
- GET /en-Latn-US/ → 200, "U!"

Context
- en-Latn-US is a valid RFC 5646 langtag (language + script + region). The language subtags are expected to be case-insensitive and the presence of both script and region should be supported by Django's i18n URL handling. I reproduced this on a fresh Django project.

Environment
- Python 3.7.5
- Django 3.2.7

Steps to reproduce (condensed)
1. startproject and add LocaleMiddleware to MIDDLEWARE
2. set LANGUAGES to include ('en-latn-us', ...) and ('en-Latn-US', ...)
3. wrap a simple view with i18n_patterns in urls.py
4. startserver and request /en-latn-us/ (404) while /en-us/ works (200)

Notes
This indicates i18n_patterns (or underlying URL matching for locale prefixes) does not accept language tags that contain both a script and a region subtag in the form shown above.

problem_statement:
Title: Make the element_id argument of json_script optional

Description:

I have a use-case where I want to use json_script to serialize JSON into a <script type="application/json"> element, but I don't need or want an id on that element. For example, when I include the <script> inside a <template> or other container, there is no need to address it by id.

Currently json_script requires an element_id argument. I can't find a security or functional reason that an id must always be provided. Making the element_id optional (e.g. defaulting to None) and omitting the id attribute when it is not given would make the helper more flexible and wouldn't break existing tests that pass an id.

Suggested behavior:
- Change the signature so element_id is optional (e.g. element_id: Optional[str] = None).
- If element_id is None or not provided, json_script should render a <script type="application/json">...</script> element with no id attribute.
- If element_id is provided, behavior should remain unchanged.

Tentative Reproducing Test:

# Starting point test — demonstrates current behavior (actual) and documents expected behavior.
# This is a pytest-style test intended as a starting point for fixing the implementation.

import json
import pytest
from django.utils.html import json_script

def test_json_script_allows_omitting_element_id():
    """
    Actual behavior:
      Calling json_script(value) without element_id currently raises a TypeError
      because the element_id argument is required.

    Desired behavior:
      Calling json_script(value) without element_id should return a script
      element with type="application/json" and no id attribute; e.g.:
        <script type="application/json">{...}</script>
    """

    data = {"a": 1}
    # Use consistent separators to match json dumps used by helpers
    expected_html = '<script type="application/json">' + json.dumps(data, separators=(",", ":")) + '</script>'

    # Actual: calling without element_id raises TypeError (current bug)
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        json_script(data)

    # The following documents the desired behavior. Marked as an explicit expected-failure
    # starting point: after making element_id optional, this assertion should be used
    # (remove the xfail) and the earlier raises(TypeError) check should be removed.
    pytest.xfail("Documenting desired behavior: json_script should accept a single 'value' argument and return script without id")
    assert json_script(data) == expected_html

Issue summary
When running Django's migration autodetector on a project that contains a custom ForeignKey subclass which hardcodes its "to" argument and removes it from deconstructed kwargs, the autodetector raises KeyError: 'to'. The failure happens during migration autodetection (generate_renamed_models / only_relation_agnostic_fields) when the code unconditionally deletes the 'to' key from the deconstructed kwargs.

What happens (symptoms)
- Running tests with verbose output triggers migration autodetection while creating the test DB.
- The autodetector raises a KeyError: 'to' and the run aborts.
- Traceback points to django/db/migrations/autodetector.py, where code does del deconstruction[2]['to'].

Root cause
A custom ForeignKey field implementation hardcodes kwargs['to'] in __init__ and deliberately removes the 'to' entry in deconstruct(). The autodetector calls field.deconstruct() and expects that the deconstructed kwargs contain a 'to' key (or at least that removing it will succeed). The autodetector code currently does:
    del deconstruction[2]['to']
which raises KeyError when the custom field's deconstruct() has already removed that key.

Why this is a problem
- Custom field authors may choose to hide or normalize parameters in deconstruct(). Removing 'to' from the deconstructed kwargs is not an invalid choice, but the autodetector should tolerate that by using a safe deletion/pop.
- A small defensive change (e.g. using pop('to', None)) would avoid the crash and make autodetection robust to custom fields that omit 'to'.

Suggested fix
Replace the unconditional delete with a safe removal, for example:
    deconstruction[2].pop('to', None)
This prevents KeyError when 'to' is missing.

Minimal reproduction
The following self-contained snippet reproduces the bug: create ProjectState before/after, add a model that has a custom ForeignKey which hardcodes and removes 'to' in deconstruct(), then run MigrationAutodetector._detect_changes(). The autodetector raises KeyError: 'to'.

Note: the test below is a starting point to reproduce the behavior programmatically. It demonstrates the actual behavior (KeyError) and documents the expected behaviour (no exception and a detected change).

Tentative Reproducing Test
# Starting point reproduction test (pytest-style).
# This test demonstrates the current/broken behavior: the autodetector raises KeyError when a custom ForeignKey
# removes the 'to' key from its deconstructed kwargs.
#
# Expected behavior: no exception; autodetector should handle missing 'to' gracefully (e.g. via pop('to', None))
# Actual behavior: KeyError: 'to'

import pytest
from django.db import models
from django.db.migrations.autodetector import MigrationAutodetector
from django.db.migrations.state import ModelState, ProjectState

class CustomFKField(models.ForeignKey):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # Hardcode the target model and pass it through to the parent
        kwargs['to'] = 'testapp.HardcodedModel'
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

    def deconstruct(self):
        name, path, args, kwargs = super().deconstruct()
        # The custom field deliberately removes 'to' from deconstructed kwargs.
        # This is allowed by custom fields, but currently breaks the autodetector.
        del kwargs["to"]
        return name, path, args, kwargs

def test_autodetector_raises_keyerror_when_fk_deconstructs_without_to():
    """
    Reproduction test:
    - Builds a before ProjectState with HardcodedModel.
    - Builds an after ProjectState that adds TestModel with CustomFKField.
    - Calling MigrationAutodetector._detect_changes() currently raises KeyError: 'to'.

    Expected: No exception and one detected migration change for 'testapp'.
    Actual: KeyError is raised. We assert that behavior here to demonstrate the bug.
    """

    before = ProjectState()
    before.add_model(ModelState('testapp', 'HardcodedModel', []))

    after = ProjectState()
    after.add_model(ModelState('testapp', 'HardcodedModel', []))
    after.add_model(
        ModelState(
            'testapp',
            'TestModel',
            [('custom', CustomFKField(on_delete=models.CASCADE))]
        )
    )

    # Demonstrate current (broken) behavior: autodetector raises KeyError('to').
    with pytest.raises(KeyError) as excinfo:
        MigrationAutodetector(before, after)._detect_changes()

    # Make the current vs expected behavior clear in assertions/messages:
    assert 'to' in str(excinfo.value), "Actual: KeyError occurred but message does not mention 'to'."
    # Expected behavior comment: if the autodetector were tolerant to missing 'to', the call above would not raise
    # and the following could be asserted:
    # changes = MigrationAutodetector(before, after)._detect_changes()

problem_statement:
When tests use @override_settings to change message tag mappings (MESSAGE_TAGS), the change is not picked up by django.contrib.messages.storage.base.Message.level_tag. The messages framework caches a module-level LEVEL_TAGS mapping at import time, so overriding settings in a test does not update that cached mapping. As a result, a Message created/read inside a test after applying @override_settings still reports an empty string (or the old tag) for level_tag instead of the new tag from the overridden MESSAGE_TAGS.

Expected behavior:
- Overriding MESSAGE_TAGS (e.g. mapping the DEBUG level to a custom tag) within a test should cause Message.level_tag to reflect that new mapping.

Actual behavior:
- Message.level_tag remains empty or reflects the original mapping because the module-level LEVEL_TAGS is not refreshed when settings are overridden in tests.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — not a final solution.
from django.test import override_settings
from django.contrib.messages.storage.base import Message
from django.contrib.messages import constants as message_constants

@override_settings(MESSAGE_TAGS={message_constants.DEBUG: 'custom-debug'})
def test_message_level_tag_not_updated_by_override_settings():
    """
    This test demonstrates that overriding MESSAGE_TAGS with @override_settings
    does not update Message.level_tag because the module-level LEVEL_TAGS mapping
    is not refreshed.

    Expected: Message.level_tag == 'custom-debug'
    Actual:   Message.level_tag == '' (or the previous value)
    """
    msg = Message(message='test', level=message_constants.DEBUG)

    expected = 'custom-debug'
    actual = msg.level_tag

    assert actual == expected, (
        f"Expected level_tag to be {expected!r} after overriding MESSAGE_TAGS, "
        f"but got {actual!r}. This indicates LEVEL_TAGS was not updated by override_settings."
    )

problem_statement:
Title: Query.change_aliases raises AssertionError when OR-ing QuerySets with overlapping generated table aliases

Summary
When OR-ing two QuerySets in Django (qs1 | qs2), Query.change_aliases can raise an AssertionError in some cases where the right-hand QuerySet has sequential table aliases that collide with aliases produced while joining. The same operation with the operands swapped (qs2 | qs1) may succeed, so the OR operation is not commutative in practice and can produce different SQL/behavior depending on operand order.

Environment
- Python: 3.9.2
- Django: reproduced on 2.2.24 and 3.2.9

What happens
Given a set of models with multiple relationships (ForeignKey and ManyToMany) the following sequence can hit an AssertionError coming from Query.change_aliases:

- Construct qs1 from a related-manager (e.g. qux.foos.all()) so it has certain table aliases.
- Construct qs2 using a filter that includes nested joins and an OR of two related filters that both traverse the same many-to-many queryset (e.g. Foo.objects.filter(Q(bars__baz__in=qux.bazes.all()) | Q(other_bars__baz__in=qux.bazes.all()))).
- Combining them with qs1 | qs2 triggers an AssertionError in Query.change_aliases because the change_map produced has keys that intersect with its values (e.g. {'T4': 'T5', 'T5': 'T6'}), implying an alias would be changed twice.

Stack trace (excerpt)
The AssertionError originates at:
  django/db/models/sql/query.py line ~854 in Query.change_aliases
with a change_map like {'T4': 'T5', 'T5': 'T6'}.

Root cause (summary)
In Query.combine when performing OR, the code attempts to rename aliases from one query to avoid collisions. If the right-hand query currently has sequential aliases (T4, T5, ...), calling Query.table_alias during joining can create aliases that cause change_map to map an alias to another alias that is itself a key in the same map. This creates a situation where an alias would need to be changed twice (T4 -> T5 and then T5 -> T6) and the assertion in change_aliases is triggered.

Expectation / Suggested fixes
- Avoid generating alias renames that result in keys intersecting values in change_map. One idea: when creating new aliases for the right-hand query during join, consult the rhs.alias_map (or rhs table aliases) to ensure any new alias suffix does not collide with existing rhs aliases — e.g., increment suffix until it is not present in rhs.alias_map.
- Consider passing the rhs alias_map into Query.join / Query.table_alias so the join logic can avoid producing conflicting aliases.
- Add a comment near the assertion explaining why keys must not intersect values (i.e., avoid double-renaming of aliases), and consider improving the AssertionError message.
- Document that QuerySet OR may not be commutative in terms of generated SQL and aliases, or make the behavior deterministic.

Reproduction notes
I reduced my project code to a minimal set of models that demonstrates the issue (see test below). The failure happens deterministically in the scenarios described above.

Tentative Reproducing Test
The following pytest-style test reproduces the assert failure. It is a starting point for debugging, not a final test or fix. It assumes the models below exist in an app accessible as bug.app.models; adapt imports/app labels to your project structure if needed.

models.py (for reference)
from django.db import models
class Foo(models.Model):
    qux = models.ForeignKey("app.Qux", on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="foos")
class Bar(models.Model):
    foo = models.ForeignKey("app.Foo", on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="bars")
    another_foo = models.ForeignKey("app.Foo", on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="other_bars")
    baz = models.ForeignKey("app.Baz", on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name="bars")
class Baz(models.Model):
    pass
class Qux(models.Model):
    bazes = models.ManyToManyField("app.Baz", related_name="quxes")

pytest test (starting point)
import pytest
from django.db.models import Q
# Import models from your app; adjust the module path as needed.
from bug.app.models import Foo, Qux

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_or_combination_alias_conflict():
    """
    Starting point test that demonstrates the AssertionError raised by Query.change_aliases.
    Expected behavior:
      - Combining qs2 | qs1 does not raise.
      - Combining qs1 | qs2 should also not raise (but currently raises AssertionError).
    Actual behavior (reproduced on Django 2.2.24 and 3.2.9):
      - qs2 | qs1 succeeds.
      - qs1 | qs2 raises AssertionError in Query.change_aliases.
    """
    # Create objects
    qux = Qux.objects.create()
    # qs1 is generated from a related manager (gives it certain table aliases)
    qs1 = qux.foos.all()
    # qs2 contains an OR of two related filters that both traverse qux.bazes
    qs2 = Foo.objects.filter(
        Q(bars__baz__in=qux.bazes.all()) | Q(other_bars__baz__in=qux.bazes.all())
    )

    # This combination currently works
    try:
        _ = qs2 | qs1
    except Exception as exc:
        pytest.fail(f"Expected qs2 | qs1 to succeed, but got exception: {exc}")

    # This combination reproduces the bug: it raises AssertionError
    with pytest.raises(AssertionError):
        # In the buggy case this line triggers an AssertionError inside Django's SQL alias change logic
        _ = qs1 | qs2

Notes:
- This test must run in a Django test environment with the models migrated. It is intended as a minimal reproduction for debugging the alias-renaming logic in Query.change_aliases / Query.join.
- Adapt the model import path if your app label is different; the original reproduction used bug.app.models.

Ömer, My initial attempt was to use Query.bump_prefix but as you told it threw an error. The error you encountered is due to bump_prefix requiring some adjustments. The alias merging algorithm that Query.combine uses requires that both query share the same initial alias in order to work otherwise you'll get a KeyError. You'll want to find a way to have bump_prefix adjust all the aliases but the initial one so it can still be used as the merge starting point. --- Vishal, Here, I am randomly choosing an uppercase letter as the first character of alias, this returns different aliases, but a test_case is failing with this approach, with the following traceback. Choosing a random initial alias will bring more bad than good as not relying on alias_prefix will cause undeterministic failures across the board. There are reasons why the prefix is used and bumped only on conflic; it makes reasoning about possible collisions easier. In 2nd approach, I have rotated the alias_prefix in a circular manner from T(class variable alias_prefix has value T) to Z, then from A to Z, and so on, and it also works on the above-attested code but fails five other test cases. This approach doesn't account for possible collisions with subquery aliases and will eventually collide once you've wrapped up around the 26 letter of the alphabet instead of using the Cartesian product approach. --- All of the required logic for preventing alias_prefix collisions already lives in bump_prefix, it's only a matter of adjusting it in order to allow it to be used in the alias merging algorithm of combine.

problem_statement:
Use simplified import paths for expression deconstruction

Description

When expression objects are deconstructed (via their deconstruct() method), the recorded import path should be the simplified path that users typically import from (django.db.models.<Name>), not the longer internal path that includes the expressions submodule (django.db.models.expressions.<Name>).

Historically, F() deconstructed to 'django.db.models.expressions.F'. A recent change made F deconstruct to 'django.db.models.F', which lets generated migration code import it as models.F when migrations use "from django.db import models". The same approach should be applied to other expression classes so generated migrations are simplified consistently.

Goal: ensure expression classes deconstruct to the short module path under django.db.models (i.e., without the ".expressions." segment) so migrations are cleaner and consistent with common import patterns.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point: a pytest that demonstrates the deconstruct path includes ".expressions." for some expressions.
# This test asserts the desired behavior (no ".expressions." in the deconstruct path) and will fail where the
# current code still uses the longer path. Use this as a starting point for fixing the deconstruct implementations.

import pytest
from django.db.models import F, Value, ExpressionWrapper, IntegerField

@pytest.mark.parametrize("instance, name", [
    (F('some_field'), "F"),
    (Value(1), "Value"),
    (ExpressionWrapper(Value(1), output_field=IntegerField()), "ExpressionWrapper"),
])
def test_expression_deconstruct_uses_simplified_path(instance, name):
    """
    Expected behavior:
      - instance.deconstruct()[0] should be a path like 'django.db.models.<Name>'
        and must not contain the '.expressions.' segment.

    Actual/buggy behavior (what this test will reveal):
      - For some expression classes the deconstruct path still contains
        'django.db.models.expressions.<Name>'.

    This test is a starting point and demonstrates expected vs actual by asserting
    that '.expressions.' is not present in the deconstruct path.
    """
    path, args, kwargs = instance.deconstruct()
    assert ".expressions." not in path, (
        f"Expected deconstruct path for {name} to omit '.expressions.' and be importable as "
        f"'django.db.models.{name}', but got: {path}"
    )

problem_statement:
Issue summary
MigrationRecorder ignores database router allow_migrate rules and creates the django_migrations table (and records migrations) on databases where the router explicitly disallows migrations.

Detailed description
We run a multi-database Django setup: one database ('default') is the project database where Django should create and manage tables; additional databases (for example 'other') are read-only external data sources with models marked managed = False. We have a simple database router that allows migrations only on the 'default' database:

class Router(object):
    def allow_migrate(self, db, model):
        if db == 'default':
            return True
        return False

When the test runner creates test databases, it iterates over all configured database connections and runs migration logic for each one. During migration, Django's executor applies migrations and calls MigrationRecorder.record_applied to note which migrations have been applied. The first thing record_applied does is call self.ensure_schema() to create the django_migrations table on that connection if it is missing.

The bug: ensure_schema() (and thus record_applied) will create the django_migrations table on every connection it is asked to use, without consulting the project's DB router allow_migrate rules. In our setup this causes django_migrations to be created on the 'other' connection, even though migrations are disallowed there by our router. The same issue likely affects other MigrationRecorder methods such as applied_migrations and record_unapplied.

Expected behavior
MigrationRecorder should respect the database router's allow_migrate rules and not create the django_migrations table or record migrations on connections where allow_migrate(db, MigrationModel) returns False. In the above router example, django_migrations should only exist on the 'default' database.

Tentative Reproducing Test
# This test is a starting point to reproduce the issue, not a final solution.
# It requires pytest-django (the `settings` fixture) and a Django test environment.

import pytest

from django.db import connections
from django.db.migrations.recorder import MigrationRecorder
from django.db import router as djrouter

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_migrationrecorder_ignores_router(settings):
    """
    Reproduces the behavior where MigrationRecorder creates the
    django_migrations table on a database even though a router disallows migrations there.

    Setup:
    - Two sqlite in-memory databases: 'default' and 'other'
    - A router that allows migrations only on 'default'
    Steps:
    - Assert django_migrations does not exist on 'other'
    - Call MigrationRecorder.record_applied(...) using the 'other' connection
    - Observe that django_migrations is created on 'other' (actual behavior)
    - Expected behavior would be that the table is NOT created on 'other' because the router disallows it.
    """

    # Configure two in-memory sqlite databases
    settings.DATABASES = {
        'default': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'NAME': ':memory:'},
        'other': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'NAME': ':memory:'},
    }

    # Simple router: allow migrations only on 'default'
    class Router:
        def allow_migrate(self, db, app_label, model_name=None, **hints):
            return db == 'default'

    # Override django's global router list for the duration of this test
    djrouter.routers = [Router()]

    other_conn = connections['other']

    # Ensure django_migrations does not exist initially on 'other'
    with other_conn.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='django_migrations';"
        )
        assert cursor.fetchone() is None, "Precondition failed: django_migrations should not exist on 'other'"

    # Create a recorder bound to the 'other' connection and record a migration as applied
    recorder = MigrationRecorder(other_conn)
    recorder.record_applied('some_app', '0001_initial')

    # Check whether django_migrations was created on 'other' after record_applied
    with other_conn.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute(
            "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name='django_migrations';"
        )
        row = cursor.fetchone()

    # Actual behavior: the table exists (this demonstrates the bug)
    assert row is not None, "Actual: django_migrations was not created on 'other' (unexpected for bug reproduction)"

    # Expected behavior (what should happen): the table should NOT be created because the router disallows migrations on 'other'
    # To assert the expected behavior instead, replace the previous assert with:
    # assert row is None, "Expected: django_migrations should not be created on 'other' due to router.allow_migrate"

problem_statement:
Issue: collapse consecutive AlterUniqueTogether / AlterIndexTogether remove/add pairs into a single operation

Description

When we split the AlterFooTogether operations (AlterUniqueTogether and AlterIndexTogether) into separate remove-then-add steps, some migrations end up containing redundant pairs of operations for the same model and same constraints. The current output can show an explicit "remove empty" pair followed by an "add new" pair, which could be safely reduced to a single operation that sets the desired final state.

Example problematic sequence:

operations = [
    migrations.AlterUniqueTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        unique_together=set(),
    ),
    migrations.AlterIndexTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        index_together=set(),
    ),
    migrations.AlterUniqueTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        unique_together={("col",)},
    ),
    migrations.AlterIndexTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        index_together={("col",)},
    ),
]

This should be optimized to:

operations = [
    migrations.AlterUniqueTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        unique_together={("col",)},
    ),
    migrations.AlterIndexTogether(
        name='mymodel',
        index_together={("col",)},
    ),
]

Rationale

- The remove-then-add split was introduced to allow intermediate field alterations to succeed, but when the net effect on a given constraint is simply "set to X" (no intermediate need), doing both remove and add is redundant.
- Collapsing those redundant pairs reduces the number of migration operations and avoids unnecessary constraint DDL.

Desired behavior

- Detect and collapse a remove-then-add pair (or more generally, sequences that cancel out intermediate states) for AlterUniqueTogether and AlterIndexTogether when it is safe to do so (i.e., when the final desired constraint set is known and no intervening operations depend on the removed state).
- Preserve behavior for cases where the intermediate remove is needed for correctness.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test: demonstrates the current undesired pattern and the expected optimized outcome.
# This is a pytest-style reproducer to be used as a starting point for implementing the optimizer change.

from django.db import migrations

def _collapse_alter_together_if_available(ops):
    """
    Try to call a real optimizer implementation if available in the codebase.
    If not available (e.g. during initial development), return the ops unchanged,
    which reproduces the current (unoptimized) behavior.
    """
    try:
        # If an optimizer function is implemented in the project, adjust this import
        # to point to it. This attempt is intentionally permissive so the test still
        # runs in environments where the function is not yet added.

problem_statement:
Description

When you annotate with a Value containing a Python str (for example, annotate(x=Value('test'))), Value._resolve_output_field() will return a CharField instance via this branch:

if isinstance(self.value, str):
    return fields.CharField()

CharField.__init__ unconditionally attaches a MaxLengthValidator even when max_length is left as None. That means a CharField constructed with no max_length ends up with a MaxLengthValidator whose limit_value is None. Using that validator then leads to a TypeError when it compares an int to None:

TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'

This happens during simple operations on the resolved output field. Example interactive session:

>>> x = Value('test')
>>> y = x._resolve_output_field()
>>> y.validators
[<django.core.validators.MaxLengthValidator at 0x...>]
>>> y.clean('1', model_instance=None)
.../django/core/validators.py in compare(self, a, b):
TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'NoneType'

There is also a small performance cost from instantiating the validator unnecessarily in the common case where no max_length is provided. Micro-benchmark numbers from one environment show:

- Baseline (CharField.__init__ as-is): ~8.1 µs per call to Value._resolve_output_field()
- Commenting out @deconstructible on validators: ~6.96 µs
- Avoiding validator instantiation entirely: ~5.86 µs

A small change to CharField.__init__ to only append MaxLengthValidator when max_length is not None matches the behavior BinaryField uses for its own validator and prevents attaching a validator that will always fail when limit_value is None. I have a local branch with that change and the existing test suite passes locally. This ticket documents the issue and includes a reproducing test to demonstrate the problem.

Tentative Reproducing Test

This pytest-style test demonstrates the current (buggy) behavior: CharField returned from Value._resolve_output_field() has a MaxLengthValidator with limit_value None, and invoking the validator (or field.clean) raises TypeError. The test is a starting point to reproduce the issue and is not a complete or final fix.

Note: This test assumes Django is importable in the test environment.

import pytest

def test_value_resolve_output_field_attaches_invalid_max_length_validator():
    from django.db.models import Value
    from django.core import validators as core_validators

    # Arrange: create a Value wrapping a Python str
    v = Value('test')

    # Act: resolve the output field that Value chooses for a Python str
    out_field = v._resolve_output_field()

    # Collect any MaxLengthValidator instances attached to the field
    max_length_validators = [
        validator for validator in out_field.validators
        if isinstance(validator, core_validators.MaxLengthValidator)
    ]

    # Expected (what we would prefer):
    # - No MaxLengthValidator should be attached when max_length is None.
    # Actual (current buggy behavior):
    assert max_length_validators, "Expected at least one MaxLengthValidator attached (reproduce failure)"

    # The attached validator has a limit_value of None, which will cause comparisons to fail.
    assert any(getattr(vld, 'limit_value', object()) is None for vld in max_length_validators), (
        "Expected a MaxLengthValidator with limit_value == None"
    )

    # Invoking the validator (or field.clean which runs validators) raises a TypeError
    # because the validator compares an int to None (1 > None).
    with pytest.raises(TypeError):
        # You can call the validator directly:
        max_length_validators[0]('1')

        # Or call the field's clean method which runs validators:
        # out_field.clean('1', model_instance=None)

# This test is a starting point to reproduce the reported bug, not a final solution.

problem_statement:
Issue summary
When applying a migration that adds a nullable OneToOneField to an existing model, SQLite (as used by Django's sqlite3 backend) raises an OperationalError: "Cannot add a UNIQUE column". This happens because Django's migration emits an ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... UNIQUE REFERENCES ... DEFERRABLE ... statement for the OneToOneField, and SQLite rejects adding a column with a UNIQUE constraint via ALTER TABLE.

Context
- Observed while running migrations for django-oauth-toolkit when upgrading from Django 4.0 to main (post-4.0) where many sqlite changes were introduced.
- Error trace (abridged): 
  django.db.utils.OperationalError: Cannot add a UNIQUE column
- Relevant migration operation that triggers the SQL:
  migrations.AddField(
      model_name='AccessToken',
      name='source_refresh_token',
      field=models.OneToOneField(blank=True, null=True, on_delete=django.db.models.deletion.SET_NULL, to=oauth2_settings.REFRESH_TOKEN_MODEL, related_name="refreshed_access_token"),
  ),

Expected behavior
- Applying the migration should succeed with SQLite. For nullable OneToOneField (which implies a nullable unique FK), the migration system should use a migration strategy that works on SQLite (for example, creating a new table, copying data, dropping old table, renaming new table), or otherwise avoid emitting an ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with a UNIQUE clause that SQLite disallows.

Actual behavior
- The migration emits an ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN statement that includes UNIQUE and REFERENCES ... DEFERRABLE, and SQLite fails with "Cannot add a UNIQUE column".

Notes
- This change surfaced between Django 4.0 and later sqlite-related patches. The failing SQL looks like:
  ALTER TABLE "oauth2_provider_accesstoken" ADD COLUMN "source_refresh_token_id" bigint NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES "oauth2_provider_refreshtoken" ("id") DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED

Tentative Reproducing Test
import sqlite3
import pytest

def test_adding_nullable_onetoone_column_fails_on_sqlite():
    """
    Starting point test that reproduces the SQLite failure described above.

    Setup:
    - Create two tables that mimic the referenced model (oauth2_provider_refreshtoken)
      and the model being altered (oauth2_provider_accesstoken).

    Action:
    - Execute the ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... UNIQUE REFERENCES ... DEFERRABLE ... SQL
      that Django currently emits for a nullable OneToOneField.

    Expected vs Actual:
    - Expected (desired): The migration step succeeds (no exception).
    - Actual (observed): sqlite3.OperationalError is raised with message
      'Cannot add a UNIQUE column'.
    """
    # Use an in-memory SQLite database
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    cur = conn.cursor()

    # Create the referenced table and the table to be altered
    cur.execute('CREATE TABLE "oauth2_provider_refreshtoken" ("id" integer PRIMARY KEY)')
    cur.execute('CREATE TABLE "oauth2_provider_accesstoken" ("id" integer PRIMARY KEY)')
    conn.commit()

    # This is the exact kind of SQL Django emits for adding a nullable OneToOneField.
    alter_sql = (
        'ALTER TABLE "oauth2_provider_accesstoken" '
        'ADD COLUMN "source_refresh_token_id" bigint NULL UNIQUE '
        'REFERENCES "oauth2_provider_refreshtoken" ("id") '
        'DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED'
    )

    # The test asserts that executing this statement raises the sqlite3.OperationalError.
    with pytest.raises(sqlite3.OperationalError) as excinfo:
        cur.execute(alter_sql)

    # Confirm the error message matches the observed message.
    assert "Cannot add a UNIQUE column" in str(excinfo.value)

# migration machinery (using MigrationExecutor or running real migrations for an app)
# would be needed to show the bug within Django's migration flow. This snippet isolates

problem_statement:
Rewritten issue description

When prefetching a related object that itself prefetches back to the original model with a different set of deferred fields, Django appears to apply the outer model's deferred-field state to the inner prefetched instances. Concretely, given two models:

class User(models.Model):
    email = models.EmailField()
    kind = models.CharField(max_length=10, choices=[("ADMIN", "Admin"), ("REGULAR", "Regular")])

class Profile(models.Model):
    full_name = models.CharField(max_length=255)
    user = models.OneToOneField(User, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

I expect to be able to:
- Query User.objects.only("email") so the outer User instances have only "email" loaded.
- Prefetch Profile objects, and for that prefetch use a Profile queryset that itself prefetches its related User with User.objects.only("kind") so those nested User instances have "kind" loaded (and not "email").

The minimal test demonstrates the intended behavior:

1) Evaluating the main queryset (User.objects.only("email").prefetch_related(...)) executes three queries:
   - SELECT user id and email for the outer User
   - SELECT profile fields for the related Profile(s)
   - SELECT inner User id and kind for the nested User prefetch

2) After the queryset is evaluated, accessing user.profile.user.kind should NOT execute any additional queries because the nested User instance already has "kind" loaded; however, in practice, accessing that attribute triggers an extra query selecting "kind" for the nested user.

Observed evidence:
- After running the main queryset, user.profile.user.get_deferred_fields() returns {'kind'}, indicating Django recorded "kind" as a deferred field for the nested user instance.
- Despite this, accessing user.profile.user.kind issues a new SELECT for the "kind" column (one extra query), which implies the instance is somehow inheriting the deferred-field set of the outer User objects instead of using the deferred fields determined when the inner User queryset ran.

This also reproduces when the relationship is a ForeignKey (accessing user.profile_set.all()[0].user.kind will trigger a similar extra query).

I'm happy to investigate and provide a patch but would appreciate confirmation that this is a bug and pointers to where to start.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point pytest test to reproduce the issue. Adapt model imports to your test app.
# This is a starting point, not a final solution.

import pytest
from django.db.models import Prefetch
from django.db import connection
from django.db.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext

# Adjust these imports to the module where your test models are defined.
from tests.models import User, Profile

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_only_related_queryset_prefetch_deferred_fields():
    # Set up objects
    user = User.objects.create(email="test@example.com", kind="ADMIN")
    Profile.objects.create(user=user, full_name="Test Tester")

    # Build queryset:
    # - Outer Users only load "email"
    # - Prefetch profile, and for each Profile prefetch its user but only load "kind"
    queryset = User.objects.only("email").prefetch_related(
        Prefetch(
            "profile",
            queryset=Profile.objects.prefetch_related(
                Prefetch("user", queryset=User.objects.only("kind"))
            ),
        )
    )

    # When evaluating the main queryset we expect three queries:
    # 1) Outer User: id + email
    # 2) Profile: id + full_name + user_id
    # 3) Inner User (prefetched for profile): id + kind
    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as ctx:
        fetched = queryset.first()
    assert len(ctx.captured_queries) == 3, (
        "Expected 3 queries when evaluating the queryset, got "
        f"{len(ctx.captured_queries)}: {[q['sql'] for q in ctx.captured_queries]}"
    )

    # Now accessing the nested user's 'kind' should NOT hit the DB because it was
    # fetched by the inner prefetch. Expected 0 queries.
    # Observed bug: this often executes 1 additional query (SELECT ... kind ...).
    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as ctx:
        assert fetched.profile.user.kind == "ADMIN"
        executed = len(ctx.captured_queries)

    assert executed == 0, (
        "Expected 0 queries when accessing nested user's deferred field, got "
        f"{executed}: {[q['sql'] for q in ctx.captured_queries]}"
    )

problem_statement:
Field.__hash__() mutates when a Field is assigned to a Model class, breaking use as a dict key.

Description

When a django.db.models.Field instance is used as a dict key and then assigned to a model class attribute, its __hash__ value changes. That breaks dictionaries and sets that previously contained the Field instance and leads to surprising crashes like the following AssertionError:

from django.db import models
f = models.CharField(max_length=200)
d = {f: 1}
class Book(models.Model):
    title = f
assert f in d  # fails because f.__hash__ changed after assignment

The change in behavior was introduced in #31750. Although few code paths create a Field and put it into a dict before assigning it to a model class, this is a valid and reasonable thing to do and the hash for an object must be immutable for it to be usable as a dict/set key. The equality fixes from #31750 are important, but mutating __hash__ is worse because it breaks existing containers.

Recommendation: revert or change the __hash__ behavior so that a Field instance has a stable hash for its entire lifetime (or at least while it can be used as a dict key). Equality can still be performed correctly without changing an object's hash after construction.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Run this in a Django test environment (pytest-django or similar).
import pytest

def test_field_hash_is_immutable_on_model_assignment():
    from django.db import models

    # Create a Field instance and put it into a dict
    f = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    d = {f: 1}
    # Sanity: before assignment, the field should be findable in the dict
    assert f in d, "Field should be present in the dict before assignment to a model."

    # Assign the same Field instance to a Model attribute
    class Book(models.Model):
        title = f

    # Expected behavior: the Field's hash remains unchanged, so it is still a key in d.
    # Actual behavior (bug): f.__hash__ changes during assignment and f is no longer found in d.
    assert f in d, (
        "Expected the field to remain in the dict after being assigned to a model class, "
        "but it was not found. This indicates Field.__hash__ changed during assignment."
    )

problem_statement:
Description

When using QuerySet.bulk_update() with a model instance attribute assigned directly to a plain F(...) expression, the F expression is not being resolved to the referenced column. Instead, the string representation of the F object ends up in the generated SQL and in the saved value.

Reproduction steps

1. Obtain a model instance with two CharField columns, for example 'name' and 'c8'.
2. Assign a plain F expression to the instance field:
   o.c8 = F('name')
3. Call bulk_update([o], ['c8'])
4. After refresh_from_db(), the saved value of c8 is the string "F(name)" rather than the current value of the name column. The UPDATE SQL contains the F() repr (e.g. 'F(name)') instead of the column reference "exampleapp_selfref"."name".

Observed SQL example:
UPDATE "exampleapp_selfref" SET "c8" = CASE WHEN ("exampleapp_selfref"."id" = 1290012) THEN 'F(name)' ELSE NULL END WHERE "exampleapp_selfref"."id" IN (1290012)

Root cause

The code path that decides whether an attribute should be treated as an expression uses a too narrow type test. As a result, plain F instances are not recognized as expressions in this code path and are stringified instead of being compiled to SQL column references.

A working check can be either a duck-typed detection (hasattr(attr, 'resolve_expression')) or an explicit isinstance check that accepts F instances in addition to Expression.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — not a final solution, only demonstrates the failing behavior.
import pytest
from django.db import connection
from django.db.models import F
from exampleapp.models import SelfRef

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_bulk_update_with_plain_F_expression_is_not_resolved():
    """
    This test demonstrates that assigning a plain F('name') to an instance field
    and saving via bulk_update results in the literal F(...) repr being stored
    instead of the referenced column value.

    Expected behavior:
      After bulk_update and refresh_from_db, obj.c8 == obj.name

    Actual behavior observed in the buggy implementation:
      obj.c8 == "F(name)" (or similar stringified repr)
    """
    # Ensure there is an instance to work with
    obj = SelfRef.objects.first()
    if obj is None:
        obj = SelfRef.objects.create(name='alice', c8='')

    # Assign a plain F expression to the instance field
    obj.c8 = F('name')

    # Perform bulk_update
    SelfRef.objects.bulk_update([obj], ['c8'])

    # Reload from database
    obj.refresh_from_db()

    # Check result
    # This assertion expresses the intended behavior. On the buggy codepath this will fail.
    assert obj.c8 == obj.name, (
        "Expected c8 to be set to the value of the 'name' column, "
        f"but got {obj.c8!r}. "
        "If failing, the generated SQL likely contains the stringified F() repr; "
        f"recent SQL (for debugging): {connection.queries[-1]['sql'] if connection.queries else 'no queries recorded'}"
    )

problem_statement:
Title: aggregate(..., default=...) after annotate(...) generates invalid SQL and crashes (SQLite example)

Description:
When using an Aggregate with the new "default" argument (added in Django 4.0) on a QuerySet that has been annotated, the ORM generates invalid SQL and the query fails. I reproduced this on Django 4.0.1 with SQLite (also observed on a PostgreSQL project).

Steps to reproduce (illustrative):
1. Have a model with rows (example uses example.core.models.Book).
2. Annotate the QuerySet (any expression), then call aggregate() with an Aggregate that includes default.

Working case (no default):
- Book.objects.annotate(idx=F("id")).aggregate(Sum("id"))
  returns: {'id__sum': 4560}

Failing case (with default):
- Book.objects.annotate(idx=F("id")).aggregate(Sum("id", default=0))
  raises: django.db.utils.OperationalError: near "FROM": syntax error

The generated SQL for the failing case (SQLite) looks like:
SELECT FROM (SELECT "core_book"."id" AS "idx", COALESCE(SUM("core_book"."id"), ?) AS "id__sum" FROM "core_book") subquery
Note the missing select list after the outer SELECT, which causes the syntax error.

Workaround:
Using Coalesce explicitly around the aggregate works:
- Book.objects.annotate(idx=F("id")).aggregate(x=Coalesce(Sum("id"), 0))
  returns: {'x': 4560}

Expected behavior:
Using the aggregate's default argument should behave like wrapping the aggregate in Coalesce; i.e. no SQL error, and the aggregate should return the same result as without default (or the default when appropriate).

Tentative Reproducing Test:
# Starting point test — adjust the import path to your project's model as needed.
import pytest
from django.db.models import Sum, F
from django.db.utils import OperationalError
# Replace this import with the appropriate model from your project
from example.core.models import Book

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_aggregate_with_default_after_annotate_raises_sqlite_error():
    """
    Reproduces the bug where using Aggregate(..., default=...) after annotate()
    produces invalid SQL (observed with SQLite) and raises OperationalError.

    Expected behavior (what should happen):
      - The call to aggregate(Sum('id', default=0)) should not raise and should
        return the same result as aggregate(Sum('id')) (or a default when no rows).

    Actual behavior (current bug):
      - aggregate(Sum('id')) works.
      - aggregate(Sum('id', default=0)) raises OperationalError (SQL syntax error).

    This test asserts the current (buggy) behavior to make reproduction easy.
    """
    # Ensure the base aggregate works
    annotated_qs = Book.objects.annotate(idx=F("id"))
    result_without_default = annotated_qs.aggregate(Sum("id"))
    assert "id__sum" in result_without_default

    # The following currently raises an OperationalError due to malformed SQL.
    # When the bug is fixed, remove the pytest.raises and assert the values match.
    with pytest.raises(OperationalError):
        annotated_qs.aggregate(Sum("id", default=0))
