It seems to me that #26565 ("Allow Prefetch query to use .values()") is related.
Hi ludwik, #26565 is about a different issue. The only way we could support slices would be to extract it from the provided queryset to make it filterable again and apply it when in-memory joining. The prefect queryset would still have to fetch all results so I'm not sure it's worth the trouble as accessing category.example_posts[:3] would have the same effect.
Charettes, Thank you for the reply. accessing category.example_posts[:3] would have the same effect I'm pretty sure that is not correct. The end effect would obviously be the same, but the way it is achieved behind the scenes and the performance characteristics that follows would be widely different. What you propose (prefetching without limit, adding slicing in a loop after the fact) would make Django perform a database query selecting all objects from the database table and loading them into memory. This would happen when the main queryset is evaluated (that's what prefetching is all about). Then the slicing would be performed by Python in memory, on a queryset that was already evaluated. That's what I understood from ​the documentation and also how Django actually behaved in an experiment I performed couple of minutes ago. What I want to avoid is exactly this behavior - loading thousands of objects from the database to display first three of them. I would be happy with a sane workaround, but to my knowledge there isn't any.
Tentatively accepting but as you've noticed it would require a large refactor of the way prefetching is actually done. I could see Category.objects.prefetch_related(Prefetch('articles', Article.object.order_by('-published_data')[0:3], to_attr='latest_articles')) being useful but the underlying prefetch query would need to rely on subqueries, a feature the ORM is not good at for now. Maybe the addition of the ​Subquery expression could help here.
The only way to limit this Query (and to not load all the records into memory) would be to do a top-n-per-group query which I don't think the ORM is capable of. What I can suggest is: Instead of limiting the QuerySet, find a way to filter it. For example, get only the Posts in the last day, week or a month (based on the post-frequency). Category.objects.prefetch_related(Prefetch( 'post_set', queryset=Post.objects.filter( date_published__gte=datetime.date.today()-timedelta(days=7)), to_attr='example_posts', )) This way you won't load all the Posts into Memory.
If window queries are implemented (https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/26608) then this use case could be possible in something similar to: Prefetch( 'post_set', queryset= Post.objects .annotate(_rank=Window(Rank(), partition_by='cateogry') .filter(_rank__lte=3) )
I tried the filter by rank suggestion using Django 2.0 but I get this error: django.db.utils.NotSupportedError: Window is disallowed in the filter clause.
I think there is a workaround now to in django new version as we have OuterRef and Subquery. from django.db.models import OuterRef, Subquery User.objects.all().prefetch_related('comments',queryset=Comment.objects.filter(id__in=Subquery(Comment.objects.filter(user_id=OuterRef('user_id')).values_list('id', flat=True)[:5])))
Note that the solution above might not be portable to some MySql databases, with error 1235, "This version of MySQL doesn't yet support 'LIMIT & IN/ALL/ANY/SOME subquery'"
As pointed out by others support for filter against window functions would allow prefetch_related_objects to use Rank(partition_by) to support this feature. If someone wants to give a shot at solving this particular issue before #28333 is resolved it should be doable by using a combination of Queryset.raw and Query.compile combinations.

problem_statement:
I have three Django apps: fonte, variavel and fonte_variavel. FonteModel and VariavelModel are related with a ManyToManyField defined on FonteModel, using FonteVariavelModel as the through model. When the through model lives in a separate app (fonte_variavel) and I run migrations, the migration that creates FonteModel raises an AttributeError: "'str' object has no attribute '_meta'".

What I expect
- Migrations should apply successfully when FonteModel defines a ManyToManyField(through="fonte_variavel.FonteVariavelModel") and the through model is declared in another app.

What actually happens
- Applying the migration that creates FonteModel fails with an AttributeError during schema creation. The traceback shows an attempt to access ._meta on the through value, but that value is a string, not a model class:
  AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute '_meta'

Relevant models (simplified)
- core/fonte/models.py
  class FonteModel(Model):
      nome = TextField(unique=True)
      descricao = TextField()
      data_inicial = DateField()
      data_final = DateField(blank=True, null=True)
      variaveis = ManyToManyField("variavel.VariavelModel", through="fonte_variavel.FonteVariavelModel")
      ...
- core/variavel/models.py
  class VariavelModel(Model):
      nome = TextField(unique=True)
      descricao = TextField()
      ...
- core/fonte_variavel/models.py
  class FonteVariavelModel(Model):
      variavel = ForeignKey('variavel.VariavelModel', on_delete=CASCADE)
      fonte = ForeignKey('fonte.FonteModel', on_delete=CASCADE)
      ...

Generated migration for FonteModel contains:
migrations.CreateModel(
    name='FonteModel',
    fields=[
        ...
        ('variaveis', models.ManyToManyField(through='fonte_variavel.FonteVariavelModel', to='variavel.variavelmodel')),
    ],
    ...
)

Notes
- If I put FonteVariavelModel inside the same app/module as FonteModel, migrations work.
- If I put FonteVariavelModel inside fonte and keep VariavelModel in variavel, it still works. The failure only occurs when the ManyToMany through model is in a separate app from FonteModel and is referenced by a string in the field declaration/migration.

Trace excerpt (relevant part)
File ".../django/db/backends/base/schema.py", line 453, in create_model
    if field.remote_field.through._meta.auto_created:
AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute '_meta'

This indicates field.remote_field.through is still a string at the time schema.create_model runs, and the code expects it to have been resolved to a model class with a _meta attribute.

Tentative Reproducing Test

Note: This is a starting point test to demonstrate the failing behavior (string through causing an AttributeError). It is not a full migration test; it isolates the exact check that raises the AttributeError.

import pytest

def test_m2m_through_string_causes_attribute_error():
    """
    Starting-point reproduction:
    Simulate a field whose remote_field.through is still a string (as can happen
    in migrations), and show that attempting to access through._meta raises
    AttributeError.

    Expected behavior (what we want):
    - The through reference should be resolved to a model class (with _meta)
      before schema code accesses through._meta, so no exception is raised.

    Actual behavior (the bug):
    - If through is still a string, accessing through._meta raises AttributeError.
    """

    class DummyRemote:
        def __init__(self, through):
            # 'through' is a string like 'fonte_variavel.FonteVariavelModel'
            self.through = through

    class DummyField:
        def __init__(self, through):
            self.remote_field = DummyRemote(through)

    # Simulate the situation created by the migration: the through is still a string.
    m2m_field_with_string_through = DummyField('fonte_variavel.FonteVariavelModel')

    # The code path in Django's schema creation effectively does:
    # if field.remote_field.through._meta.auto_created: ...
    # Since through is a str, accessing _meta should raise AttributeError.
    with pytest.raises(AttributeError):
        # This line reproduces the exact failure observed in the traceback.
        _ = m2m_field_with_string_through.remote_field.through._meta

    # For contrast, show the expected (resolved) case does not raise:
    class FakeModel:
        class _meta:
            auto_created = True

    m2m_field_with_model_through = DummyField(FakeModel)
    # Accessing _meta succeeds when through is an actual model-like object.
    assert hasattr(m2m_field_with_model_through.remote_field.through, '_meta')

# End of tentative test - starting point only.

problem_statement:
Issue summary

When using the __in lookup with a QuerySet that has both annotate() and alias() called, the subquery generated for the IN clause does not reduce to a single selected column (the Book primary key). Instead the subquery keeps the annotated/aliased selected columns, causing the SQL sub-select to return multiple columns and raising an OperationalError like:

django.db.utils.OperationalError: sub-select returns 10 columns - expected 1

Expected behavior

Filtering with ModelA.objects.filter(fk__in=some_qs) should generate a subquery that selects only the single column required for the IN comparison (normally the primary key of the right-hand-side model). Calling annotate().alias() on the RHS queryset must not cause extra columns to be included in that subquery.

Reproduction steps (summary)

1. Build a RHS queryset that filters Book objects, then calls annotate() and alias() on it.
2. Use that queryset in a Publisher.objects.filter(book__in=RHS_qs).values("name") query.
3. Executing the Publisher query raises an OperationalError because the subquery returns multiple columns instead of one.

Concrete minimal example (conceptual)

    long_books_qs = (
        Book.objects.filter(pages__gt=400)
        .annotate(book_annotate=Value(1))
        .alias(book_alias=Value(1))
    )
    publisher_books_qs = Publisher.objects.filter(book__in=long_books_qs).values("name")
    # Executing publisher_books_qs raises:
    # django.db.utils.OperationalError: sub-select returns 10 columns - expected 1

Why this is a bug

The ORM should generate the subquery for the IN lookup to only include the single column needed for comparison. annotate() and alias() are allowed on the RHS, but they should not change the set of selected columns used by the IN subquery.

Tentative Reproducing Test

This is a starting point test (not a final solution). It is written in pytest style and uses Django's ORM. Replace 'yourapp' with the actual app label containing the Book and Publisher models if necessary.

from django.apps import apps
import pytest
from django.db.utils import OperationalError
from django.db import transaction
from django.db.models import Value

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_annotation_and_alias_filter_in_subquery_raises_operational_error():
    """
    Starting point test to reproduce the bug:
    - Expected behavior: the query returns publisher names for publishers that have books with pages > 400.
    - Actual behavior (bug): executing the query raises an OperationalError about the sub-select returning multiple columns.
    """

    # Adjust this app label to where Book and Publisher are defined in your project
    Book = apps.get_model('yourapp', 'Book')
    Publisher = apps.get_model('yourapp', 'Publisher')

    # Create publishers
    apress = Publisher.objects.create(name='Apress')
    sams = Publisher.objects.create(name='Sams')
    ph = Publisher.objects.create(name='Prentice Hall')
    mk = Publisher.objects.create(name='Morgan Kaufmann')
    other = Publisher.objects.create(name='OtherPub')

    # Create books (some with pages > 400 to be included in long_books_qs)
    Book.objects.create(title='B1', pages=500, publisher=apress)
    Book.objects.create(title='B2', pages=450, publisher=sams)
    Book.objects.create(title='B3', pages=600, publisher=ph)
    Book.objects.create(title='B4', pages=420, publisher=mk)
    # Some books that should not match
    Book.objects.create(title='B5', pages=200, publisher=other)

    long_books_qs = (
        Book.objects.filter(pages__gt=400)
        .annotate(book_annotate=Value(1))
        .alias(book_alias=Value(1))
    )

    publisher_books_qs = Publisher.objects.filter(book__in=long_books_qs).values("name")

    # Expected result (what should happen): query returns the four publisher names
    expected = {'Apress', 'Sams', 'Prentice Hall', 'Morgan Kaufmann'}

    # Actual behavior: executing the queryset should raise an OperationalError about the sub-select.
    # We wrap in a transaction to ensure DB error is surfaced cleanly in some DB backends.
    with pytest.raises(OperationalError) as excinfo:
        with transaction.atomic():
            list(publisher_books_qs)  # execution triggers SQL; on bug this raises OperationalError

    assert 'sub-select returns' in str(excinfo.value), (
        "Expected an OperationalError indicating the sub-select returned multiple columns, "
        f"got: {excinfo.value!s}"
    )

    # Note: If the ORM is fixed, running `list(publisher_books_qs)` should return:
    # assert set(item['name'] for item in list(publisher_books_qs)) == expected

We have some simplification in the __in lookup that automatically limit selected fields to the pk when Query is on the right-side and the selected fields are undefined. It looks like they don't play nice when .annotate() and .alias() are mixed. Tentatively accepted for the investigation.
Whether or not the In lookups defaults a Query right-hand-side to .values('pk') is based of rhs.has_select_fields (​source) This dynamic property is based of self.select or self.annotation_select_mask so I suspect that there might be some bad logic in Query.add_annotation (​source) from the introduction of QuerySet.alias in f4ac167119e8897c398527c392ed117326496652. The self.set_annotation_mask(set(self.annotation_select).difference({alias})) ​line seems to be what causes the problem here. If annotate and alias are used then annotation_select_mask will be materialized as a mask is required to keep track of which entries in annotations must be selected and whatnot (not necessary if only using alias or annotate as the first doesn't require any selecting and the second selects all annotations) The add_annotation logic relied on to implement QuerySet.alias is not wrong per se it just happens to piggy back on the annotation masking logic that only Query.set_values relied on previously an now happens to break the heuristics in Query.has_select_fields. The proper solutions is likely to replace Query.has_select_fields by a class attribute that defaults to False and have set_values set it to True and make sure Query.clone carries the attribute over. This seems like a more durable options as that avoids trying to peek into internals to determine if a values call was performed. Gabriel, since you've already written a regression test, would you be interested in submitting a patch that takes the approach proposed above?

problem_statement:
When using the modulo (MOD) operator in a Django query expression that mixes numeric types (for example, a DecimalField with an IntegerField), Django fails to resolve the expression's output_field to a DecimalField. For other arithmetic operators (Add, Subtract, Multiply, Divide) Django correctly infers a Decimal output when a Decimal operand is present, but the MOD operator currently ends up resolving to an Integer output field (or otherwise not resolving to Decimal), which can lead to incorrect type handling downstream.

Steps and effect:
- Given a model with a DecimalField and an IntegerField.
- Construct an expression that computes decimal_field % integer_field (using F expressions and the % operator).
- After resolving the expression's output_field, the result is not a DecimalField as expected; other arithmetic operators do resolve to DecimalField when a Decimal operand participates.

This causes queries and annotations that rely on correct numeric typing (e.g., for database casting, aggregate types, or serializer expectations) to behave incorrectly when % is used with mixed numeric types.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — not a final solution
# This pytest-style test demonstrates the expected vs actual behavior.
# It constructs a minimal model, builds a modulo expression mixing Decimal and Integer fields,
# resolves the expression's output_field, and asserts the expected Decimal resolution.
# The test uses a local model with app_label to avoid migrations.

import pytest
from django.db import models
from django.db.models import F, DecimalField, IntegerField

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_mod_operator_resolves_to_decimal_output_field():
    class TempModel(models.Model):
        decimal = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)
        integer = models.IntegerField()

        class Meta:
            app_label = "tests_mod"
            # Keep migrations out of the way for this ephemeral test
            managed = False

    # Build the modulo expression: decimal % integer
    mod_expr = F('decimal') % F('integer')

    # Trigger resolution of output_field using the model's _meta
    # In normal query construction, Django will call resolve_output_field;
    # here we invoke it explicitly to inspect what type is assigned.
    mod_expr.resolve_output_field(TempModel._meta)

    # Expected behavior: because one operand is Decimal, the result should be DecimalField.
    # Actual behavior observed: the resolved output_field is not a DecimalField.
    assert isinstance(mod_expr.output_field, DecimalField), (
        "Expected modulo expression of (DecimalField % IntegerField) to resolve to DecimalField, "
        f"but got {type(mod_expr.output_field)!r} instead."
    )

# Note: This test is a starting point to reproduce the issue. Depending on Django version,
# import locations or APIs may vary; adjust the test harness accordingly.

problem_statement:
The Django admin changelist view (ModelAdmin.changelist_view) handles editing multiple rows at once when using list_editable. That processing can write multiple objects to the database in one HTTP POST. If one of those saves fails partway through (for example due to a validation error or an exception raised in a signal/clean/save hook), the current code may leave some rows updated and others unchanged because the entire changelist POST is not wrapped in a transaction.atomic() context. In other words, partial commits are possible, which can leave the database in an unexpected, inconsistent state.

This should be addressed by wrapping the list_editable processing in a transaction so that either all edited rows are saved, or none are (the whole request is rolled back) when an error occurs.

# Starting point pytest-style test to reproduce the reported bug.
# Notes:
# - This is a minimal starting point. You will need a Django project with:
#   - an app `myapp`
#   - a model `MyModel` in `myapp.models` with at least fields: id (AutoField), name (CharField), flag (BooleanField)
#   - MyModel registered in the admin with list_editable = ('flag',)
# - The exact admin form field names and management form values may need minor adjustments depending on Django version.
# - The intent: simulate an exception during saving of the second row and assert whether the first row's change was committed (actual) vs the expected all-or-nothing rollback.
import pytest
from django.urls import reverse
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.db.models.signals import pre_save
from django.dispatch import receiver
from django.test import Client
from myapp.models import MyModel  # adjust to your app/model

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_changelist_list_editable_not_atomic_leads_to_partial_commit():
    """
    Starting-point test that demonstrates the changelist list_editable processing
    can leave partial commits if a save fails mid-way.

    Expected behavior (what we want): If one row fails to save during list_editable
    processing, none of the rows should be changed (atomic behavior).

    Actual behavior (the bug being reported): If the view is not wrapped in a transaction,
    the first row(s) already saved remain changed while later saves fail, leaving a partial update.
    """

    # Create a superuser and log in to the admin
    User = get_user_model()
    admin_username = "admin"
    admin_password = "password123"
    User.objects.create_superuser(admin_username, "admin@example.com", admin_password)
    client = Client()
    assert client.login(username=admin_username, password=admin_password)

    # Create two objects to edit in the changelist
    obj1 = MyModel.objects.create(name="object-1", flag=False)
    obj2 = MyModel.objects.create(name="object-2", flag=False)

    # Connect a pre_save signal that raises an exception when saving obj2 to simulate a failure.
    def fail_on_obj2(sender, instance, **kwargs):
        if instance.pk == obj2.pk:
            raise RuntimeError("simulated failure during save")

    pre_save.connect(fail_on_obj2, sender=MyModel)

    try:
        # Build a POST payload that mimics the admin changelist formset for list_editable.
        # The formset management fields are standard; adjust if your Django version differs.
        post_data = {
            # Formset management form
            'form-TOTAL_FORMS': '2',
            'form-INITIAL_FORMS': '2',
            'form-MIN_NUM_FORMS': '0',
            'form-MAX_NUM_FORMS': '1000',
            # Row 0 (obj1) - change flag to True
            'form-0-id': str(obj1.pk),
            'form-0-flag': 'on',  # boolean fields are typically represented like this from a checkbox
            # Row 1 (obj2) - change flag to True (but the save will raise)
            'form-1-id': str(obj2.pk),
            'form-1-flag': 'on',
            # Depending on Django version/admin, you may also need to include the changelist "index" or submit name:
            # 'index': '0',
            # '_save': 'Save',  # sometimes admin checks for a "save" submit name
        }

        changelist_url = reverse('admin:myapp_mymodel_changelist')  # adjust names to your app/model
        response = client.post(changelist_url, post_data, follow=True)
    finally:
        # Always disconnect the signal to avoid side effects for other tests
        pre_save.disconnect(fail_on_obj2, sender=MyModel)

    # Reload objects from the database to observe what was committed.
    obj1.refresh_from_db()
    obj2.refresh_from_db()

    # Expected (correct transactional behavior): both objects remain unchanged (flag=False)
    expected_obj1_flag = False
    expected_obj2_flag = False

    # Actual (observed when changelist_view is NOT wrapped in a transaction): obj1 was saved, obj2 failed.
    actual_obj1_flag = obj1.flag
    actual_obj2_flag = obj2.flag

    # Assert and show clear expected vs actual. This assertion documents the bug.
    assert (actual_obj1_flag, actual_obj2_flag) == (expected_obj1_flag, expected_obj2_flag), (
        "Bug detected: changelist list_editable processing allowed a partial commit.\n"
        f"Expected flags (obj1, obj2): ({expected_obj1_flag}, {expected_obj2_flag}) but "
        f"got: ({actual_obj1_flag}, {actual_obj2_flag}).\n"
        "If obj1 changed while obj2 did not, the changelist view needs to wrap list_editable processing "
        "in a transaction.atomic() to ensure all-or-nothing behavior."
    )

problem_statement:
makemigrations --check creates migration files instead of only checking

Description

When scripting a check for missing migrations, I expect makemigrations --check to perform a dry check and exit without creating any migration files. However, unlike migrate --check and optimizemigration --check (which only exit and do not write files), makemigrations --check will still write migration files to disk unless --dry-run is also provided.

This behavior is inconsistent and surprising: the --check flag on makemigrations should behave like the other commands and simply report whether migrations are needed, without writing files. I couldn't find any discussion of this design choice in ticket 25604 or the linked developer thread. The documentation is silent on whether --check should create files; currently it requires both --check and --dry-run to avoid writing migrations, which seems wrong.

Expected: makemigrations --check exits (non-zero if migrations would be created) but does not create migration files.
Actual: makemigrations --check leaves migration files on disk unless --dry-run is also specified.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point pytest test (not a final solution)
# This test demonstrates the reported inconsistency: running makemigrations --check for a new app
# causes migration files to be written. The test asserts the expected behavior (no files created)
# and shows the actual behavior (files created).
#
# Notes:
# - This is intended as a minimal reproducible test to demonstrate the bug. CI environments might
#   require adjustments (e.g. Python path, Django settings, or isolation).
# - The test configures a minimal Django settings object and creates a temporary app on disk.

import io
import os
import sys
import importlib
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

import django
from django.conf import settings
from django.core.management import call_command

def test_makemigrations_check_does_not_write_files(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    # Arrange: create a minimal Django app on disk
    app_dir = tmp_path / "testapp"
    app_dir.mkdir()
    (app_dir / "__init__.py").write_text("")  # make it a package

    # apps.py with AppConfig to ensure Django recognizes the app
    (app_dir / "apps.py").write_text(
        "from django.apps import AppConfig\n\n"
        "class TestappConfig(AppConfig):\n"
        "    name = 'testapp'\n"
    )

    # models.py with a simple model so makemigrations would normally create an initial migration
    (app_dir / "models.py").write_text(
        "from django.db import models\n\n"
        "class Item(models.Model):\n"
        "    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)\n"
    )

    # Ensure the temporary app is importable
    sys.path.insert(0, str(tmp_path))
    # Clear any cached import of testapp
    if "testapp" in sys.modules:
        del sys.modules["testapp"]

    # Minimal settings required for makemigrations to run
    if not settings.configured:
        settings.configure(
            INSTALLED_APPS=["testapp"],
            DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},
            SECRET_KEY="test-secret-key",
            USE_I18N=False,
            USE_L10N=False,
            USE_TZ=False,
            ROOT_URLCONF="",
        )
    django.setup()

    migrations_dir = app_dir / "migrations"

    # Ensure migrations directory does not exist before running the command
    if migrations_dir.exists():
        # Remove it to start clean
        for f in migrations_dir.iterdir():
            f.unlink()
        migrations_dir.rmdir()
    assert not migrations_dir.exists(), "migrations directory should not exist before the test"

    # Act: run makemigrations with --check and capture output
    out = io.StringIO()
    # call_command may raise SystemExit in some Django versions when --check is used and changes are detected.
    # We catch SystemExit to allow the test to continue to the filesystem assertions.
    try:
        call_command("makemigrations", "--check", stdout=out, stderr=out)
    except SystemExit:
        # Some management command implementations exit with a non-zero code to indicate changes were needed.
        pass

    output = out.getvalue()

    # Assert expected behavior: no migration files were created when using --check.
    # This is the behavior we want to enforce; currently the actual behavior is that files are written.
    expected_no_migrations = True
    actual_migrations_created = migrations_dir.exists() and any(
        p.name.endswith(".py") and p.name != "__init__.py" for p in migrations_dir.iterdir()
    )

    # The test records both expected and actual so failing behavior is clear.
    assert expected_no_migrations, "Test expectation: makemigrations --check should not create migration files"
    assert not actual_migrations_created, (
        "Actual behavior: makemigrations --check created migration files. "
        f"Command output:\n{output}\n"
        f"Created files: {list(migrations_dir.iterdir()) if migrations_dir.exists() else 'None'}"
    )

problem_statement:
Issue summary
When a Django View subclass defines only an async handler (for example, async def post), sending a GET request to that view raises a TypeError instead of returning a normal 405 Method Not Allowed response. The exception message is: "object HttpResponseNotAllowed can't be used in 'await' expression".

What happens
- Define a View subclass with only an async post method.
- Register it with path("demo", Demo.as_view()).
- Sending a GET request to /demo (which is not implemented on the view) results in a server error (500) and the following traceback fragment:

TypeError: object HttpResponseNotAllowed can't be used in 'await' expression

This suggests that the internal dispatch logic is trying to await a synchronous HttpResponseNotAllowed instance, which raises a TypeError in async contexts. The expected behavior is to return a 405 HttpResponseNotAllowed response to the client.

Minimal reproducer (concept)
views.py:
from django.views import View
from django.http import HttpResponse

class Demo(View):
    """Supports only POST (async), no GET"""
    async def post(self, request):
        return HttpResponse("ok")

urls.py:
from django.urls import path
from .views import Demo

urlpatterns = [
    path("demo", Demo.as_view()),
]

Reproduction steps
1. Create an empty Django 4.1.1 project with Python 3.10.
2. Add the Demo view and URL above.
3. Run the development server (manage.py runserver) and open http://127.0.0.1:8000/demo in a browser.
4. Instead of a 405 response, the server crashes with the TypeError shown above.

Expected behavior
- GET /demo should respond with an HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed response (HttpResponseNotAllowed), not raise a TypeError.

Actual behavior
- A TypeError is raised when the framework attempts to await an HttpResponseNotAllowed object.

Tentative Reproducing Test
Below is a pytest-style test (starting point) that attempts to reproduce the problem using Django's AsyncClient and an inline URLConf. It demonstrates the expected behavior (returning a 405 response) versus the observed behavior (TypeError mentioning HttpResponseNotAllowed). This is a minimal starting point for a test; it assumes pytest-django is installed and configured.

import pytest
from django.test import AsyncClient, override_settings
from django.urls import path
from django.views import View
from django.http import HttpResponse

# Minimal async-only view: only POST is implemented as async
class Demo(View):
    async def post(self, request):
        return HttpResponse("ok")

# Expose urlpatterns for override_settings(ROOT_URLCONF=__name__)
urlpatterns = [
    path("demo", Demo.as_view()),
]

@pytest.mark.asyncio
@override_settings(ROOT_URLCONF=__name__)
async def test_get_on_async_post_view_behaviour():
    """
    Starting point test:
    - Expected: GET /demo returns a 405 HttpResponseNotAllowed (status_code == 405).
    - Observed in the reported bug: the request raises TypeError about awaiting HttpResponseNotAllowed.
    This test currently asserts the observed behavior to make the failure explicit.
    Adjust assertions to match expected behavior when the bug is fixed.
    """
    client = AsyncClient()

    # Observed behavior in the bug report: a TypeError is raised when performing GET
    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as excinfo:
        await client.get("/demo")

    # Confirm that the TypeError message mentions HttpResponseNotAllowed,
    # which indicates an attempt to 'await' a synchronous response object.
    assert "HttpResponseNotAllowed" in str(excinfo.value)

    # If the bug is fixed, the following (uncommented) assertions would be the expected outcome:
    # response = await client.get("/demo")
    # assert response.status_code == 405
    # assert b"Method Not Allowed" in response.content

Note: This test is a starting point to reproduce the issue in a pytest-django environment. Depending on your test runner and Django test configuration, you may need to adapt settings or use a different client setup. The important part is that a GET request to an async-only View currently triggers a TypeError instead of returning a 405 response.

problem_statement: When the User admin change page is reached from another model's admin that references User via a non-primary lookup field (i.e., using to_field, for example to_field="uuid"), the User change view URL looks like: .../user/22222222-3333-4444-5555-666677778888/change/?_to_field=uuid However, the help text for the read-only password field in the UserChangeForm builds a relative link to the password change form using a hard-coded "../password/" path. The relevant portion of the form behaves like this: class UserChangeForm(forms.ModelForm): password = ReadOnlyPasswordHashField( label=_("Password"), help_text=_( "Raw passwords are not stored, so there is no way to see this " "user’s password, but you can change the password using " 'this form.' ), ) ... def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) password = self.fields.get("password") if password: password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") ... Because the change view may be accessed with an object identifier that is not the model instance's primary key (due to _to_field being used), using "../password/" produces an incorrect link and can lead to a 404 when the "this form" link is followed. The link should take into account the actual identifier used in the URL for the current object, or at least point to the password form for the current instance. A simple improvement is to include the actual instance identifier in the generated link, for example: password.help_text = password.help_text.format(f"../../{self.instance.pk}/password/") This makes the link point to the expected password-change URL for the current instance even when the admin was reached via a non-pk to_field. problem_statement:
Description

The Django runserver command documents that passing "0:8000" is equivalent to "0.0.0.0:8000" (i.e. listen on all interfaces). However, when I start the development server using the shorthand address "0:8000", the startup message prints an invalid URL:

$ python manage.py runserver 0:8000
Watching for file changes with StatReloader
...
Starting development server at http://0:8000/
...

The printed address "http://0:8000/" is not a usable link in a browser and is inconsistent with the documented equivalence. The startup message should show the expanded address "http://0.0.0.0:8000/" when the user passes "0:8000" on the command line so it matches the docs and produces a valid URL.

Steps to reproduce
- In a Django project directory containing manage.py, run:
  python manage.py runserver 0:8000
- Observe the "Starting development server at ..." line in stdout.

Expected behaviour
- The startup message should read:
  Starting development server at http://0.0.0.0:8000/

Actual behaviour
- The startup message reads:
  Starting development server at http://0:8000/

Tentative Reproducing Test

# This is a starting point test (not a final solution).
# It launches "python manage.py runserver 0:8000 --noreload", captures the startup line,
# then kills the process. Adjust timeouts/cwd as appropriate for your environment.

import os
import re
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time

import pytest

def test_runserver_prints_expanded_address(tmp_path):
    """
    Start the Django development server with the shorthand address "0:8000",
    capture the "Starting development server at ..." output line, and assert
    that the printed host is the expanded form "0.0.0.0" rather than "0".

    This test is a starting point: it assumes you run it from the project root
    (where manage.py lives) and that running the command is permitted in the
    test environment. It uses a timeout and forcibly terminates the server
    process after reading the line.
    """
    manage_py = os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "manage.py")
    if not os.path.exists(manage_py):
        pytest.skip("manage.py not found in current working directory; adjust cwd for this test")

    cmd = [sys.executable, "manage.py", "runserver", "0:8000", "--noreload"]
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        cmd,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        bufsize=1,
        universal_newlines=True,
    )

    try:
        start_time = time.time()
        timeout = 10.0  # seconds
        found_line = None
        pattern = re.compile(r"Starting development server at (http://[^/]+:\d+/)")
        while True:
            # Timeout guard
            if time.time() - start_time > timeout:
                pytest.fail("Timeout while waiting for runserver startup line")

            line = proc.stdout.readline()
            if not line:
                # Short sleep to avoid busy loop; if process exited, break
                if proc.poll() is not None:
                    break
                time.sleep(0.1)
                continue

            m = pattern.search(line)
            if m:
                found_line = m.group(1)
                break

        assert found_line is not None, "Did not find 'Starting development server at ...' in output"

        expected = "http://0.0.0.0:8000/"
        actual = found_line

        # Demonstrate expected vs actual: if the command prints "http://0:8000/",
        # this assertion will fail and show the mismatch.
        assert actual == expected, f"Expected '{expected}' but got '{actual}'"

    finally:
        # Ensure the server process is terminated
        try:
            if proc.poll() is None:
                proc.send_signal(signal.SIGINT)
                # give it a moment to exit
                time.sleep(0.5)
                if proc.poll() is None:
                    proc.kill()
        except Exception:
            pass
        proc.stdout.close()

problem_statement:
Summary
Related managers (the objects you get from reverse/forward relations, e.g. instance.related_set) incorrectly got async helper methods acreate(), aget_or_create(), and aupdate_or_create() that were added when making QuerySet async-compatible. Those methods were wired up to call the QuerySet implementations (e.g. QuerySet.create()) instead of the related-manager implementations (e.g. RelatedManager.create()). As a result, relation-specific logic (setting the foreign-key on new instances, handling through tables/routing, etc.) is bypassed, and operations through the related manager can fail or produce incorrect objects.

What happened
A change that added an async-compatible interface to QuerySet also (unintentionally) added async methods to related managers. The related-manager acreate(), aget_or_create(), and aupdate_or_create() implementations simply call the QuerySet methods via sync_to_async(self.create) / sync_to_async(self.get_or_create) / sync_to_async(self.update_or_create) instead of delegating to the related manager's own create/get_or_create/update_or_create. Because related managers augment/override those operations to inject relation-specific behavior (for example, adding the FK value or applying write routing), calling the QuerySet implementation from the related manager misses that behavior.

Where to look
The problematic code is in django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py where the related-manager factories add async wrappers that call the QuerySet methods, e.g.:

    async def acreate(self, **kwargs):
        return await sync_to_async(self.create)(**kwargs)

This occurs in both forward and reverse related manager creators (many-to-one and many-to-many descriptors), so there are multiple places that need proper fixes.

Expected fix
Related managers should provide their own async wrappers that call the related-manager implementation (self.create / self.get_or_create / self.update_or_create) in a way that preserves the relation-specific behavior. Concretely, replace the current sync_to_async(self.create) usage that resolves to a QuerySet method with a sync_to_async call that invokes the related manager's method (or otherwise ensure the related-manager path is used).

Impact
When using the async helpers on a related manager (e.g. await parent.children.acreate(...)), the resulting behavior can be incorrect: the created child may lack its FK to parent or an IntegrityError may be raised because the FK was not set. This breaks expectations of the related-manager API and is a regression introduced by the async QuerySet changes.

problem_statement:
When calling QuerySet.count() on a queryset that has annotations, Django still includes those annotations in the SQL it generates even when those annotations are not used by any filters, other annotations, or ordering. For example:

Book.objects.annotate(Count('chapters')).count()

produces the same numeric result as:

Book.objects.count()

but the SQL emitted for the first form still contains the COUNT('chapters') expression (or references the related table), which is unnecessary for computing the overall count. Leaving unused annotations in the count() query can add complexity and cost to the SQL (e.g., additional joins or GROUP BYs) for no reason. select_related is already ignored by count(), so Django could similarly strip out annotations that are not referenced elsewhere in the queryset when producing the count() SQL. Stripping unused annotations would speed up count() calls that start from complex annotated querysets.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — adjust app/model names as needed
# This pytest-style test demonstrates the reported behavior by inspecting the SQL executed when calling count().
# Assumes you have a Book model and a Chapter model with a FK from Chapter to Book and a related_name='chapters'.
# Replace 'yourapp' with the actual app label containing Book and Chapter.

import pytest
from django.apps import apps
from django.db.models import Count
from django.db import connection
from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_count_includes_unused_annotation_in_sql():
    Book = apps.get_model('yourapp', 'Book')
    Chapter = apps.get_model('yourapp', 'Chapter')

    # create minimal data so count() issues a real query
    b = Book.objects.create(title='Sample')
    Chapter.objects.create(book=b, title='C1')

    # Run count() on a queryset that has an annotation which is not used elsewhere
    qs = Book.objects.annotate(Count('chapters'))

    # Capture the SQL executed by count()
    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as captured:
        total = qs.count()

I have also run into problems with QuerySet.count() being very slow on annotated query sets. Django uses a subquery for the count but injects a group by into the subquery. This typically causes the database server to deduplicate all matched rows using the group by columns which is, in general, extremely slow when there are a large number of matched rows. For example, consider the following model: class Person(models.Model): """Person model.""" first_name = models.TextField() last_name = models.TextField() country = models.TextField(null=True, blank=True) and query set: from django.db.models.functions import Concat from django.db.models import Value queryset = Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')) queryset.count() generates the following query under PostgreSQL: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT "support_person"."id" AS Col1, CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "support_person" GROUP BY "support_person"."id", CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name"))) subquery list(queryset) generates: SELECT "support_person"."id", "support_person"."first_name", "support_person"."last_name", "support_person"."country", CONCAT("support_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "support_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "support_person" I am not entirely sure why the subquery for the count needs to be any different from the query used when the query set itself is evaluated. There are some relevant comments in the source code here: ​https://github.com/django/django/blob/5deb7a86e8b54d052a3b1dbed1ae7142d362b1c5/django/db/models/sql/query.py#L404-L414 This has all been tested under Django 2.1.7.
This is somewhat related to #30158 where the compiler is not smart enough to determine if it can exclude subquery annotations from GROUP BY on aggregation.
The behaviour is actually a bit more bizarre than I thought. With the same person model, here are four count variations and the generated queries: 1. Person.objects.count() SELECT COUNT(*) AS "__count" FROM "people_person" 2. Person.objects.values('pk').count() SELECT COUNT(*) AS "__count" FROM "people_person" 3. Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')).count() SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT "people_person"."id" AS Col1, CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "people_person" GROUP BY "people_person"."id", CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) ) subquery 4. Person.objects.annotate(full_name=Concat('first_name', Value(' '), 'last_name')).values('pk').count() SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT "people_person"."id" AS Col1 FROM "people_person") subquery So there's a simple workaround for the case I gave in my last comment in calling .values('pk') before .count(). However, that's not much help if Django or other libraries are the ones calling .count(). On the plus side, I have a better understanding of what the problem is from looking at the Django source code.
Just a note to say that the behaviour I was describing was rectified in ​https://github.com/django/django/pull/11062. The third case from above now executes the following SQL query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT CONCAT("people_person"."first_name", CONCAT(' ', "people_person"."last_name")) AS "full_name" FROM "people_person" ) subquery Although the original ticket was about eliminating unneeded annotations completely, the result above is good enough for me, as the group by has been eliminated which was the real performance killer.

problem_statement:
When using QuerySet.bulk_create(..., update_conflicts=True, update_fields=[...], unique_fields=[...]) on a model that defines db_column with mixed-case names, the generated ON CONFLICT clause uses the model field names (lowercase Python attribute names) instead of the actual database column names defined by db_column. That produces invalid SQL for PostgreSQL when the actual database column names are mixed-case and quoted.

Example model (fields use db_column with mixed case):
class ActivityBlackListed(models.Model):
    class Meta:
        db_table = "Activity_BlackListed"
    blacklistid = models.IntegerField(primary_key=True, db_column="BlacklistID")
    sectorid = models.IntegerField(null=True, blank=True, db_column="SectorID")
    ...

Observed behavior:
- The INSERT portion of the generated SQL correctly uses the db_column names:
  INSERT INTO "Activity_BlackListed" ("BlacklistID", ...) VALUES (%s, ...)

- The ON CONFLICT / DO UPDATE portion incorrectly uses the Python field names (lowercase), not the db_column names:
  ON CONFLICT("blacklistid") DO UPDATE SET "sectorid" = EXCLUDED."sectorid", ...
  PostgreSQL then errors with: ERROR: column "blacklistid" does not exist

Expected behavior:
- The ON CONFLICT clause should use the actual database column names (db_column), preserving case and quoting them consistently with the INSERT:
  ON CONFLICT("BlacklistID") DO UPDATE SET "SectorID" = EXCLUDED."SectorID", ...

This mismatch between which identifier is used for the INSERT and ON CONFLICT parts makes the SQL invalid when db_column differs from the field name (especially when mixed-case and quoted identifiers are involved).

# This test captures the SQL produced by bulk_create with update_conflicts=True and asserts

# Marked as a starting point — you may need to adapt the model import and test settings (pytest-django) for your project.

from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext
from django.db import connection

# Replace this import with the model in your project that sets db_column on fields.

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_bulk_create_on_conflict_uses_db_column_names():
    """
    Reproducing test for bulk_create(update_conflicts=True) generating ON CONFLICT using
    model field names instead of db_column names.

    Expected:
      - Generated SQL uses the actual database column names (db_column), e.g.
        ON CONFLICT("BlacklistID") DO UPDATE SET "SectorID" = EXCLUDED."SectorID"

    Actual (buggy behavior reported):
      - Generated SQL uses the Python field names, e.g.
        ON CONFLICT("blacklistid") DO UPDATE SET "sectorid" = EXCLUDED."sectorid"
    """

    # Prepare a single instance to insert/update
    inst = ActivityBlackListed(blacklistid=1, sectorid=42)

    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as captured:
        # This is the call that should generate an ON CONFLICT clause.
        # It currently produces incorrect SQL when db_column differs from field name.
        ActivityBlackListed.objects.bulk_create(
            [inst],
            update_conflicts=True,
            update_fields=["sectorid"],     # intentionally using the Python field name
            unique_fields=["blacklistid"],  # intentionally using the Python field name

    actual_bad_on_conflict = 'ON CONFLICT("blacklistid")'
    actual_bad_update_set = '"sectorid" = EXCLUDED."sectorid"'

    # Assert expected behavior. If this assertion fails, it shows the bug reproduces.
    assert expected_on_conflict in sql and expected_update_set in sql, (

        "Expected to find (example):\n"
        f"  {expected_on_conflict} ... {expected_update_set}\n\n"
        "But found (buggy case example):\n"
        f"  {actual_bad_on_conflict} ... {actual_bad_update_set}\n"
    )

problem_statement:
When using django.contrib.auth.forms.UserCreationForm with a custom User model that defines ManyToManyField relations, the selected values for those related fields are not saved when the form is saved with commit=True. The root cause is that UserCreationForm.save(commit=True) does not call self.save_m2m(), unlike django.forms.ModelForm.save(). As a result, any ModelMultipleChoiceField or other m2m-backed fields created by the ModelForm are ignored and their relationships are not persisted.

This was discussed on the django-developers mailing list (https://groups.google.com/u/1/g/django-developers/c/2jj-ecoBwE4). I can work on a pull request to fix this by ensuring UserCreationForm.save() forwards save_m2m() when commit=True.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test — requires a test project where AUTH_USER_MODEL points to a custom user model
# that defines a ManyToManyField called `tags` (to a Tag model in the same app).
# The following pytest-style test demonstrates the expected vs actual behavior.
# It is a starting point and may need adjustments to match your test app layout.

import pytest
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.contrib.auth.forms import UserCreationForm
from django.test import Client

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_usercreationform_saves_many_to_many_field():
    """
    Preconditions for this test to run in your test project:
    - settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL points to a custom user model (e.g. "accounts.CustomUser")
    - That custom user model has a ManyToManyField named `tags` pointing to a Tag model.
    - The Tag model is migrateable and available in the test database.

    What this test does:
    - Creates two Tag instances.
    - Submits a UserCreationForm with username/password and the tags selected.
    - Calls form.save(commit=True) and inspects the saved user's tags.

    Expected behavior (what we assert):
    - The saved user should have both tags associated (saved_user.tags.count() == 2).

    Actual/buggy behavior being reported:
    - Because UserCreationForm.save() omits save_m2m(), the related tags are not saved
      (saved_user.tags.count() == 0).

    This test will fail (showing the bug) if the tags are not saved. If the framework
    already calls save_m2m() in your Django version, the test will pass.
    """

    User = get_user_model()
    # Create two tag instances. Replace 'myapp.Tag' with the actual Tag model import
    from django.apps import apps
    Tag = apps.get_model('myapp', 'Tag')  # adjust 'myapp' and 'Tag' to match your test project

    tag1 = Tag.objects.create(name="alpha")
    tag2 = Tag.objects.create(name="beta")

    form_data = {
        'username': 'alice',
        'password1': 'complex-password-123',
        'password2': 'complex-password-123',
        # ManyToMany fields are submitted as a list of primary keys.
        'tags': [tag1.pk, tag2.pk],
    }

    form = UserCreationForm(data=form_data)
    assert form.is_valid(), "Form should be valid in the reproducing scenario"

    user = form.save(commit=True)

    # Expected: 2 tags associated.
    expected_count = 2
    actual_count = user.tags.count()

    # The test asserts the intended / expected behavior.
    assert actual_count == expected_count, (
        f"Expected {expected_count} tags on the saved user, "
        f"but found {actual_count}. This shows save_m2m() was not called by UserCreationForm.save()."
    )

problem_statement:
timesince() raises TypeError when USE_TZ=True for intervals of one month or more

Description

After commit 8d67e16493c9..., calling django.utils.timesince.timesince() with a datetime that is one month (or longer) in the past causes a TypeError when the project setting USE_TZ is True.

Reproduction summary:
- timezone.now() returns an aware datetime when USE_TZ=True.
- Subtracting a datetime.timedelta of >= 31 days produces an aware datetime input to timesince().
- timesince() constructs a "pivot" datetime internally that is offset-naive (no tzinfo).
- The subtraction of an aware datetime and an offset-naive datetime raises:
  TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes

This appears to be caused by the pivot creation not respecting the tzinfo of the supplied datetime. Passing the tzinfo (e.g. d.tzinfo) into the pivot datetime constructor fixes the TypeError locally.

problem_statement:
floatformat crashes when formatting "0.00" with precision 0

Summary:
Calling Django's floatformat filter with a value of "0.00" (as a string or a Decimal) and precision 0 raises a ValueError instead of returning a formatted "0" (or otherwise performing the expected formatting).

Reproduction (minimal):
from decimal import Decimal
from django.template.defaultfilters import floatformat

floatformat('0.00', 0)             # raises ValueError
floatformat(Decimal('0.00'), 0)    # raises ValueError

Observed behavior:
Both calls raise:
ValueError: valid range for prec is [1, MAX_PREC]

Expected behavior:
Formatting a zero value with precision 0 should succeed and return a reasonable formatted string, e.g. "0" (or at least not raise ValueError). The filter should accept 0 as a valid precision for zero values.

problem_statement:
When a FileField is constructed with a storage argument that is a callable, the field's deconstruct() method should include a reference to that callable in the returned kwargs so migrations can record it. However, if the callable happens to return django.core.files.storage.default_storage, deconstruct() currently omits the storage kwarg entirely.

Background:
- The bug occurs because FileField.deconstruct() checks whether self.storage is not default_storage to decide whether to include storage in the deconstructed kwargs.
- At deconstruct time, self.storage is the evaluated storage (the result of calling the callable), not the original callable object. If the callable returns default_storage, that check evaluates to False and the storage kwarg is dropped.
- As a result, repeatedly running makemigrations on a model that uses a callable storage which sometimes returns default_storage can cause migrations to randomly include or omit the storage argument. The storage argument should always be preserved as a reference to the callable, regardless of what the callable returns.

Example that triggers the problem:
from django.core.files.storage import FileSystemStorage, default_storage
from django.db import models
import random

other_storage = FileSystemStorage(location='/media/other')

def get_storage():
    return random.choice([default_storage, other_storage])

class MyModel(models.Model):
    my_file = models.FileField(storage=get_storage)

Running makemigrations repeatedly may produce migrations that randomly include or omit storage=myapp.models.get_storage on the FileField.

Tentative Reproducing Test:
Note: This test is a starting point to reproduce the issue; it may need to be adapted to your test harness (e.g. ensuring Django settings are configured and django.setup() has been called).

import django
import pytest
from django.conf import settings

def test_filefield_deconstruct_preserves_callable_storage():
    # Ensure minimal settings for default_storage to exist.
    if not settings.configured:
        settings.configure(DEFAULT_FILE_STORAGE='django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage')
    django.setup()

    from django.core.files.storage import default_storage
    from django.db.models import FileField

    # Callable that returns the default storage. Under the reported bug,
    # deconstruct() will omit the storage kwarg because it compares the
    # evaluated storage (default_storage) to default_storage.
    def get_storage_returning_default():

problem_statement:
After upgrading to Django 1.10, the development server (runserver) returns response bodies for HTTP HEAD requests.

Description

Per RFC 2616 (section 4.3), servers must not return a message-body in response to HEAD requests; the server is supposed to send the same headers as for GET but omit the body. In PR #26052 Django stopped stripping response bodies for HEAD requests in the framework code, on the assumption that WSGI servers (gunicorn, mod_wsgi, etc.) already perform the body removal. However, the built-in development server (runserver) does not perform this stripping and therefore returns the full response body for HEAD requests. This makes runserver non-compliant with the specification starting in Django 1.10 and can cause "Broken pipe" errors in runserver logs when clients (correctly) close the connection after receiving headers.

Steps to reproduce (from the original report)
1) Create virtualenv and install Django 1.10.x:
   mkvirtualenv django-test
   pip install 'Django>1.10,<1.11'
2) Start a new project:
   django-admin startproject django-test
   cd django-test
3) Run the development server:
   ./manage.py runserver
4) From another terminal, make a HEAD request:
   curl -iX HEAD http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Expected response (headers only, no body):
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: ...
Server: WSGIServer/0.2 CPython/3.x
Content-Type: text/html
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

Actual response (contains the HTML body as well):
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Date: ...
Server: WSGIServer/0.2 CPython/3.x
Content-Type: text/html
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">...
(or whatever the GET body would contain)

Notes
- Reported against Django 1.10; behavior is not present in 1.9.13.
- Tested on Python 2.7.13 and 3.4.5.

Tentative Reproducing Test

# Starting point test (pytest-style). This test creates a minimal Django project in a temporary directory,
# launches runserver in a subprocess, sends a raw HEAD request, and asserts that no response body is returned.
# This is intended as a starting point for reproduction and may need tweaks in CI environments or to handle
# timing and port availability more robustly.

import os
import sys
import socket
import subprocess
import time
import textwrap
import tempfile
import shutil

import pytest

def _write_file(path, content):
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(content)

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="Flaky on Windows due to process handling; adjust as needed.")
def test_runserver_head_request_should_not_return_body(tmp_path):
    # Arrange: create a minimal Django project layout that runserver can run.
    project_dir = tmp_path / "proj"
    project_dir.mkdir()
    manage_py = project_dir / "manage.py"
    proj_pkg = project_dir / "myproject"
    proj_pkg.mkdir()
    (proj_pkg / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    # Minimal settings: DEBUG=True, ROOT_URLCONF points to urls below.
    settings_py = textwrap.dedent("""
        SECRET_KEY = 'test'
        DEBUG = True
        ROOT_URLCONF = 'myproject.urls'
        ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']
        INSTALLED_APPS = []
    """)
    _write_file(proj_pkg / "settings.py", settings_py)
    urls_py = textwrap.dedent("""
        from django.conf.urls import url
        from django.http import HttpResponse

        def index(request):
            return HttpResponse('<html><body>HELLO</body></html>')

        urlpatterns = [
            url(r'^$', index),
        ]
    """)
    _write_file(proj_pkg / "urls.py", urls_py)
    manage_py.write_text(textwrap.dedent("""
        #!/usr/bin/env python
        import os
        import sys

        if __name__ == '__main__':
            os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'myproject.settings')
            from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
            execute_from_command_line(sys.argv)
    """))
    # Make manage.py executable just in case
    os.chmod(str(manage_py), 0o755)

    # Find a free port to avoid collisions.
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    host, port = sock.getsockname()
    sock.close()

    # Start runserver in subprocess
    env = os.environ.copy()
    env["PYTHONUNBUFFERED"] = "1"
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        [sys.executable, str(manage_py), "runserver", f"127.0.0.1:{port}"],
        cwd=str(project_dir),
        env=env,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
        universal_newlines=True,
    )

    try:
        # Wait for server to start (simple approach: poll output)
        started = False
        start_deadline = time.time() + 10.0
        while time.time() < start_deadline:
            line = proc.stdout.readline()
            if not line:
                time.sleep(0.1)
                continue
            if "Starting development server at" in line or "Quit the server with CONTROL-C" in line:
                started = True
                break
        assert started, "runserver did not start in time; output:\n" + (proc.stdout.read() or "")

        # Act: send a raw HEAD request and read raw response
        s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", port), timeout=5)
        try:
            # Send HTTP/1.1 HEAD request
            req = "HEAD / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n"
            s.sendall(req.encode("ascii"))
            received = b""
            while True:
                chunk = s.recv(4096)
                if not chunk:
                    break
                received += chunk
        finally:
            s.close()

        # Decode safely
        try:
            text = received.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        except Exception:
            text = str(received)

        # Split headers and body by first double CRLF
        parts = text.split("\r\n\r\n", 1)
        headers = parts[0]
        body = parts[1] if len(parts) > 1 else ""

        # Assert: per RFC, body should be empty for HEAD. If runserver returns a body, that's the bug.
        # Expected: body == "" (no content). Actual (on affected Django versions): body contains HTML like "<!DOCTYPE html>" or "HELLO".
        assert body == "", (
            "Expected no response body for HEAD, but got a body. This reproduces the reported issue.\n"
            "---- HEAD response headers ----\n"
            f"{headers}\n"
            "---- HEAD response body (truncated) ----\n"
            f"{body[:500]!s}"
        )
    finally:
        # Tear down: ensure we terminate the server process
        try:
            proc.terminate()
        except Exception:
            pass
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=5)
        except Exception:
            proc.kill()
            proc.wait(timeout=5)
        # Clean up temp project dir is handled by pytest's tmp_path

# Note: This test is a starting point. In CI or other environments you may need to:
# - Adjust timeouts and server-readiness checks.
# - Ensure Django is importable in the test environment.
# - Run on a non-Windows platform or adapt process handling for Windows.

problem_statement:
Issue summary
The template tag that decides whether to show the "Save as new" button in the Django admin does not check for the user's add permission. Because of that, a staff user who has change permission but not add permission can still see the "Save as new" button on the change form.

Details
File: django/contrib/admin/templatetags/admin_modify.py
Around line 102, the context value "show_save_as_new" is computed for the admin change form. The current code does not include a check for the user's add permission. "Save as new" creates a new object from the current object, so it should only be shown to users who have the add permission for that model.

Proposed fix suggestion (what I applied in my project)
Add an extra check for has_add_permission when computing "show_save_as_new". For example:
"show_save_as_new": (
    not is_popup
    and has_add_permission  # this additional check is required
    and has_change_permission
    and change
    and save_as
),

Reasoning
Without the has_add_permission check, users who only have change permission but not add permission will be presented with a UI action that they are not authorized to perform. This is confusing and can lead to authorization inconsistencies.

Tentative Reproducing Test
The following pytest-style test is a starting point to demonstrate the bug: it registers a ModelAdmin with save_as=True for the User model, creates a staff user with change permission but without add permission, opens the change form for an existing object, and asserts that the "Save as new" button should not be visible. With the current behavior (missing has_add_permission check), the test will find the "Save as new" button and fail, demonstrating the issue.

Note: This is a starting point, not a final solution. It assumes pytest-django and a normal Django test environment.

import pytest
from django.contrib import admin
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.contrib.auth.models import Permission
from django.contrib.contenttypes.models import ContentType
from django.test import Client

@pytest.mark.django_db
def test_save_as_new_requires_add_permission():
    """
    Starting point test demonstrating that the "Save as new" button is shown
    even when the user lacks add permission.

    Expected behavior:
      - A staff user who has change permission but does NOT have add permission
        SHOULD NOT see the "Save as new" button on the change form.

    Actual behavior (bug):
      - The "Save as new" button is displayed despite the lack of add permission.
    """

    User = get_user_model()
    client = Client()

    # Ensure the User admin uses save_as=True for this test.
    # Unregister any existing registration and register a simple admin with save_as=True.
    try:
        admin.site.unregister(User)
    except Exception:
        # If it wasn't registered, ignore
        pass

    class UserAdminWithSaveAs(admin.ModelAdmin):
        save_as = True

    admin.site.register(User, UserAdminWithSaveAs)

    # Create a staff user that will access the admin (not a superuser).
    staff_user = User.objects.create_user(username='staff', password='pw')
    staff_user.is_staff = True
    staff_user.save()

    # Grant only the change permission for User, intentionally do NOT grant add permission.
    content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(User)
    change_perm = Permission.objects.get(content_type=content_type, codename='change_' + User._meta.model_name)
    staff_user.user_permissions.add(change_perm)
    staff_user.save()

    # Create an object to edit (the object shown in the change form).
    obj = User.objects.create_user(username='target', password='pw')

    # Log in as the staff user and GET the admin change page for the object.
    client.force_login(staff_user)
    change_url = f'/admin/{User._meta.app_label}/{User._meta.model_name}/{obj.pk}/change/'
    response = client.get(change_url)

    content = response.content.decode('utf-8')

    # The admin change form renders a "Save as new" control with name="_saveasnew".
    has_save_as_new = 'name="_saveasnew"' in content or 'Save as new' in content

    # Expected: the button should NOT be present because the user lacks add permission.
    assert not has_save_as_new, (
        "Expected the 'Save as new' button to be hidden for users without add permission, "
        "but it was present. This demonstrates the missing has_add_permission check in the template context."
    )

problem_statement:
Summary
When a FormSet has can_delete=True and can_delete_extra=False, calling add_fields() with index=None (for example via FormSet.empty_form()) raises a TypeError because the code compares index (None) to an int. The comparison index < initial_form_count fails when index is None.

Details
- Conditions:
  - A FormSet is constructed with can_delete=True and can_delete_extra=False.
  - add_fields() is called with index=None (this happens when accessing FormSet.empty_form()).
- Symptom:
  - TypeError: "'<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'int'".
- Root cause:
  - In django/forms/formsets.py the code does:
    if self.can_delete and (self.can_delete_extra or index < initial_form_count):
  - When index is None, the expression index < initial_form_count raises the TypeError.
- Proposed fix:
  - Ensure index is not None before comparing to initial_form_count:
    if self.can_delete and (self.can_delete_extra or (index is not None and index < initial_form_count)):

Minimal reproduction
- Create a formset factory with can_delete=True and can_delete_extra=False.
- Instantiate the formset with initial=None.
- Access formset.empty_form — this triggers add_fields() with index=None and raises the TypeError.

Tentative Reproducing Test
The following pytest-style test demonstrates the reported bug. It is a starting point for a regression test and not a final solution.

import pytest
import django
from django import forms
from django.conf import settings

def _configure_django_once():
    if not settings.configured:
        # Minimal settings needed to import and use django.forms
        settings.configure(DEBUG=True, SECRET_KEY="test", ROOT_URLCONF=__name__)
        django.setup()

def test_formset_add_fields_index_none_raises_typeerror():
    """
    Starting point test: demonstrates that accessing FormSet.empty_form raises
    TypeError when can_delete=True and can_delete_extra=False and the formset
    is created with initial=None (so add_fields() gets index=None).

    Expected behavior: accessing empty_form should NOT raise.
    Actual behavior (current bug): a TypeError is raised because None is compared to int.
    """
    _configure_django_once()

    class MyForm(forms.Form):
        my_field = forms.CharField()

    MyFormSet = forms.formset_factory(
        form=MyForm,
        can_delete=True,
        can_delete_extra=False,
    )

    my_formset = MyFormSet(initial=None)

    # Expected: no exception when accessing empty_form.
    # Actual: a TypeError is raised; assert that behavior to reproduce the bug.
    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as excinfo:
        _ = my_formset.empty_form

    # The message can vary by Python version; check for key substrings that indicate the None vs int comparison.
    msg = str(excinfo.value)
    assert ("NoneType" in msg and "int" in msg) or ("not supported" in msg and "<" in msg)

problem_statement:
Description

I have a sequence of migration operations that modify the same field multiple times:

operations = [
    migrations.AddField(
        model_name="book",
        name="title",
        field=models.CharField(max_length=256, null=True),
    ),
    migrations.AlterField(
        model_name="book",
        name="title",
        field=models.CharField(max_length=128, null=True),
    ),
    migrations.AlterField(
        model_name="book",
        name="title",
        field=models.CharField(max_length=128, null=True, help_text="help"),
    ),
    migrations.AlterField(
        model_name="book",
        name="title",
        field=models.CharField(max_length=128, null=True, help_text="help", default=None),
    ),
]

When I run the migration optimizer on the full list, the optimizer reduces the sequence down to a single AddField (which is expected, because all the Alters apply to the newly added field). However, if the AddField is not included in the input to the optimizer (for example because the AddField lives in a separate non-elidable migration or in a migration that is not being squashed), then the optimizer does not collapse the consecutive AlterField operations at all:

optimizer.optimize(operations[1:], "books")
# returns three AlterField operations instead of a single combined AlterField

In other words, multiple consecutive AlterField operations on the same field are not being reduced/merged when no preceding AddField is present in the operations list. The implementation of AlterField.reduce appears to not consider the case where the previous operation is also an AlterField on the same field.

Is this behavior intended? If not, would it make sense to treat consecutive AlterField operations on the same field as reducible (e.g., keep only the last AlterField)? If it is intended, could this be documented?

A possible change would be to have AlterField.reduce recognize a previous AlterField that targets the same field and return only the latter operation.

problem_statement:
AdminSite.catch_all_view is dropping the query string when it issues a redirect for trailing-slash normalization (APPEND_SLASH=True).

What happens
- When a request with a query string hits the admin catch-all (for example, /admin/auth/foo?id=123) and settings.APPEND_SLASH is True, AdminSite.catch_all_view issues a redirect to the path with a trailing slash.
- The redirect currently discards the original query string, so the Location header becomes /admin/auth/foo/ instead of /admin/auth/foo/?id=123.

Why this is a problem
- Query parameters are significant for many admin views and for downstream code. Losing them on the redirect changes semantics of the request and can break functionality or links that rely on those parameters.

Concrete example
- Request:  http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/foo?id=123
- Expected redirect (preserve query string): http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/foo/?id=123
- Actual redirect produced by AdminSite.catch_all_view: http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/auth/foo/

Root cause
- The redirect is constructed from request.path and does not append request.META['QUERY_STRING'] (or otherwise preserve request.GET). The code returns something like:
  return HttpResponsePermanentRedirect("%s/" % request.path)
  which drops the query string.

Tentative Reproducing Test
This is a starting point pytest-style test demonstrating the reported behavior. It constructs a RequestFactory GET request with a query string and calls admin.site.catch_all_view directly. The test asserts the redirect Location should include the original query string but (with the current behavior) it will not.

Note: This is a minimal reproduction to illustrate the failing behavior and is intended as a starting point for a proper test case.

from django.test import RequestFactory, override_settings
from django.contrib import admin
import pytest

@override_settings(APPEND_SLASH=True)
def test_admin_catch_all_view_preserves_query_string():
    """
    Starting-point test: calling admin.site.catch_all_view with a request
    containing a query string should produce a redirect that preserves the
    query string (i.e. '/admin/auth/foo/?id=123'), but currently the redirect
    drops the query string (i.e. '/admin/auth/foo/').
    """
    rf = RequestFactory()
    # Simulate a request to the admin catch-all with a query string
    request = rf.get('/admin/auth/foo?id=123')
    # Sanity check: the query string is present on the request
    assert request.META.get('QUERY_STRING') == 'id=123'

    # Call the catch-all view directly (app_label='auth', object_name='foo')
    response = admin.site.catch_all_view(request, 'auth', 'foo')

    # Expected behavior: preserve query string when appending slash
    expected_location = '/admin/auth/foo/?id=123'

    # Actual behavior observed: query string is dropped
    # The assertion below is the one that will fail with the current implementation,
    # demonstrating the bug.
    assert response.status_code == 301
    assert response['Location'] == expected_location
